So the men who walked into that arena walked in as career professionals negotiating a fee and a seat beside the throne. Hold that picture, because by the end of the passage they will be asking a different Lord for a different reward.

Ibn Kathir frames the whole encounter with a principle. The Egyptians wanted to extinguish the Light of Allah with their words, but Allah insisted that His Light should prevail even though the disbelievers disliked it. This, he says, is the issue of disbelief and faith: they never confront one another but faith always prevails. He cites Allah's words, "Nay, We fling the truth against the falsehood, so it destroys it, and behold, it disappears" (21:18), and "Truth has come and falsehood has vanished" (17:81).

## "Cast whatever you wish to cast" — and the oath they swore

Musa's opening line looks strange at first. Is a prophet telling people to perform sorcery?

Ma'arif ul Qur'an answers this directly. On a cursory look one might be inclined to think that Musa (peace be upon him) ordered them to perform their magic. But with a little deeper thought it becomes clear that this was not an order to *show magic*; the real intention was to demonstrate the fallacy of magic, and that demonstration was not possible without the magic they showed. Therefore he asked them to show their tricks. Ma'arif gives a clarifying comparison: it is exactly like a *zindiq* (an extreme heretic) being asked to put forward his arguments so that they may be countered. Obviously, it says, such an invitation cannot be treated as an acceptance of unbelief.

That is a useful principle for anyone who studies or debates falsehood: letting an argument be stated in full so it can be dismantled is not endorsing it. Notice too the confidence in Musa's tone. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel in Surah Ta Ha, where the magicians offered him the choice — "O Musa! Either you throw first or we be the first to throw?" — and he replied, "Nay, throw you first!" (20:65-66). He gives falsehood the first move, and still it loses.

So they threw their ropes and their staffs, and swore an oath: *bi-'izzati Fir'awn* — "by the might of Fir'awn, it is we who will certainly win."

Ibn Kathir's comment is short and cutting: this is what the ignorant masses say when they do something — *this is by the virtue of So-and-so.* From other places in the Qur'an he fills in what their display actually was. In Surat al-A'raf, "they bewitched the eyes of the people, and struck terror into them, and they displayed a great magic" (7:116). In Surah Ta Ha, "their ropes and their sticks, by their magic, appeared to him as though they moved fast" (20:66) — running on until Allah's words, "and the magician will never be successful, whatever the amount of skill he may attain" (20:69). It was real fear and real spectacle, but it worked on eyes.

**Ma'arif ul Qur'an takes this oath as a ruling.** Swearing "by the majesty of the Pharaoh" was an expression of pledge from the magicians which was in vogue in the olden times. It is unfortunate, the commentary says, that similar oaths have now become common among Muslims as well, and are even more evil and vile — "by the king," "by the head of yours," "by the beard of yours," "by the grave of your father." It is not permitted to make an oath of this nature under Islamic law, because swearing in the name of someone other than Allah is a sin. Ma'arif goes further, citing *Ruh*: it will not be wrong to say that swearing a *true* oath in this way is as sinful as swearing a *false* oath in the name of Allah.

This is one of the most concretely applicable points in the passage. Oaths are a form of reverence. To hang your word on the honour of a person, a grave, a beard, or a head is to give something a weight that belongs to Allah alone — and the magicians' oath shows exactly where that instinct leads. They staked everything on Fir'awn's might, and Fir'awn's might could not save their ropes from being swallowed.

## The staff, and the men on the ground

"Then Musa threw his stick, and behold, it swallowed up all that they falsely showed."

The Arabic verb is *talqafu*, and Ibn Kathir explains it as snatching up and catching them from every corner and swallowing them up, so that it did not leave any of them untouched. This was not a superior trick that outshone theirs; it was a total consumption of theirs, leaving nothing on the ground. And what it swallowed is described as *ma ya'fikun* — "all that they falsely showed." The ropes and sticks were real objects; what moved was shown falsely to the eyes.

Ibn Kathir then quotes the parallel account in Surat al-A'raf: "Thus truth was confirmed, and all that they did was made of no effect," running through to "the Lord of Musa and Harun" (7:118-122). He calls this a very serious matter, furnishing decisive proof and leaving no room for any excuse. Fir'awn's supporters, who sought and hoped that they would prevail over Musa, were themselves defeated.

Then the ayah that turns the whole passage: "And the sorcerers fell down prostrate." Ibn Kathir describes what happened at that moment — they believed in Musa and prostrated to Allah, the Lord of al-'Alamin, the Lord of all the worlds, Who sent Musa and Harun with the truth and an obvious miracle.

This is worth sitting with. The crowd saw a wonder; the professionals saw the end of their profession. The people who had come to watch a competition could only judge the result; the men who had spent their lives producing illusions knew exactly what they had just failed to produce.

Notice also how they phrase it. First the universal claim: "We believe in the Lord of al-'Alamin." Then the identification: "the Lord of Musa and Harun." Ma'arif ul Qur'an underlines the setting of that declaration — these were men who had believed Fir'awn's claim to be a god and used to worship him, and they pronounced faith in Allah before that tyrannical, despotic king and the entire nation. Naming Musa and Harun's Lord in that place left no ambiguity about which Lord they meant.

## Threats that only deepened faith

Fir'awn's response is a case study in how power behaves when it has lost the argument. Ibn Kathir says he was defeated in a manner the likes of which the world had never seen, but he remained arrogant and stubborn despite the clear evidence — may the curse of Allah and the angels and all of mankind be upon him. He resorted to arrogance and stubbornness and propagating falsehood.

**First, he changes the subject to authority.** "You have believed in him before I give you leave" — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, *you should have asked my permission for what you did and you did not consult with me; if I had given you permission you could have done it, and if I did not allow you, you should not have done it, for I am the ruler and the one to be obeyed.* He does not argue that the miracle was false. He complains that belief was not licensed. Truth is treated as a matter requiring official clearance.

**Second, he invents a conspiracy.** "Surely, he indeed is your chief, who has taught you magic." Ibn Kathir dismisses this as stubborn talk that anyone can see is nonsense: they had never met Musa before that day, so how could he have been their chief who taught them how to do magic? No rational person would say this. But a crowd whose people were followers of the religion of their king does not need such a story to be plausible.

**Third, when neither works, he threatens the body.** He threatened to cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and to crucify them all.

And here Ibn Kathir gives the key to their steadiness. His threats against them, he says, resulted only in an increase in their faith and their submission to Allah — for the veil of disbelief had been lifted from their hearts and the truth became clear to them, because they knew something that their people did not: that what Musa had done could not have been done by any human being unless Allah helped him, making it a proof and an evidence of the truth of what he had brought from his Lord. Their expertise is precisely what left them no room to pretend. Threats could reach their bodies but not that knowledge.

## "No harm"

Their answer is two words in Arabic: *la dayr*. Ibn Kathir glosses it: "no problem, that will not harm us and we do not care."

Then the reason: "Surely, to our Lord we are to return." This means, Ibn Kathir says, that the return of us all is to Allah, may He be glorified, and He will never allow the reward of anyone who has done good to be lost; what you have done to us is not hidden from Him, and He will reward us in full for that. Ma'arif ul Qur'an renders the gist of their reply this way: *you do whatever you can; we shall lose nothing. Even if we are killed we will go back to our Lord, where there is nothing but comfort.*

Then they add hope: "Verily, we really hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins." Ibn Kathir specifies what sins they had in mind — the sins they had committed, and the magic Fir'awn had forced them to do. And "as we are the first of the believers" means, he says, because they were the first of their people, the Egyptians, to believe.

Look at what they are now asking for. Earlier the same men had asked Fir'awn, "Will there surely be a reward for us if we are the winners?" and were promised a place among those who sit close to him. Now they seek something from a different Master, and what they want is not a seat beside a king but forgiveness. They are no longer negotiating; they are hoping.

**Ma'arif ul Qur'an dwells on how astonishing this is.** These were men who had spent all their lives practising sinful sorcery, who had believed Fir'awn's claim to be a god and even used to worship him — and they pronounced faith in Allah before that tyrant and despotic king and the entire nation. That in itself was something most astonishing and courageous. But it was not just a pronouncement of faith: it was a demonstration of such deep devotion that it was as if they could see the Last Day and the Hereafter before their eyes. The blessings and bounties of the Hereafter were within their sight, and so they raised themselves over and above any punishment or torment of this world and said, as Surah Ta Ha records, "You do whatever you are to do" (20:72) — *we are not going back from our faith.*

Ma'arif then makes a point that reframes the whole passage: this transformation was itself a miracle of Musa (peace be upon him), no less than the miracle of the staff and the luminous hand. The staff changed what was on the ground; this changed what was in their hearts. The commentary adds that many incidents of a similar nature also occurred with our Prophet ﷺ — in one such incident a drastic change occurred in a seventy-year-old disbeliever, who within a minute not only accepted Islam but was ready to lay down his life as a martyr.

Ibn Kathir closes the episode in four words: **so he killed them all.** The Qur'an does not linger on it, and neither should we — except to notice that Fir'awn did to them exactly what he threatened, and that by their own reckoning it took from them nothing, since the return of them all was to Allah, Who never allows the reward of anyone who has done good to be lost.

## What this passage asks of us

- **Do not swear by anything but Allah.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an makes this the practical fruit of the magicians' oath, naming the oaths people still use — by the king, by your head, by your beard, by your father's grave — and ruling them impermissible in Islamic law.
- **Follow evidence, not the winning side.** "That we may follow the sorcerers if they are the winners" is the exact posture the magicians abandoned once the proof reached them. Ibn Kathir's diagnosis of the crowd — followers of the religion of their king — is a warning about where our loyalties quietly attach.
- **A sinful past is not a verdict.** Lifelong sorcerers who had worshipped a false god became the first believers of Egypt, and openly hoped their Lord would forgive them everything behind them.
- **Threats can measure faith rather than defeat it.** Ibn Kathir's observation that Fir'awn's threats "resulted only in an increase in their faith" is the passage in one line: what falsehood uses to break people, Allah can use to raise them.

passages.title: The night exodus and the tyrants drawn out
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the hinge of the story of Musa (peace be upon him) in this sūrah: the long confrontation in Egypt is over, and now Allah moves. In eight ayat we watch a people slip out of Egypt by night on a divine command, a furious king mobilise an empire to chase them, and — before we are told anything about how the pursuit ended — Allah announce the outcome: the tyrants lost everything, and the people they had dismissed inherited it.

What holds ayat 52–59 together is a single reversal, told in the order the Qur'an wants us to feel it. Ayah 52 is Allah's command and Allah's warning. Ayat 53–56 are Fir'awn's voice — the only speech in the passage, and it is all boasting. Ayat 57–59 are Allah's voice again, closing the account. The tyrant speaks in the middle; Allah speaks first and last.

## What comes just before

Ibn Kathir sets the scene: Musa (peace be upon him) had stayed in Egypt "for a long time," and through that long stay the proof of Allah was established against Fir'awn and his chiefs. They still refused, "still arrogant and stubborn." At that point, Ibn Kathir says, "there was nothing left for them but punishment and vengeance." So ayah 52 does not open a new argument. It closes the door on argument. When a people have seen the evidence and hardened anyway, the next thing is not another sign — it is the sentence.

The immediately preceding scene sharpens this. Fir'awn had just threatened his own magicians with death, mutilation and crucifixion for believing, and they answered without flinching, *"There is no harm. We are to return to our Lord"* (26:50). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes how astonishing this was: men who had spent their lives in sorcery, who had believed Fir'awn's claim to be a god and even worshipped him, now declared faith in Allah before that tyrant and the whole nation — and not merely declared it, but showed a devotion so deep it was as though the Hereafter were before their eyes, so that they set themselves above any punishment of this world. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this in itself a miracle granted to Musa (peace be upon him), no less than the miracle of the staff or the luminous hand. Fir'awn had already lost the argument in his own court. Ayah 52 is what follows a loss like that.

## Ayah 52 — "Depart by night with My servants"

Ibn Kathir renders the command: **"Depart by night with My servants, verily, you will be pursued."** Allah commanded Musa (peace be upon him), in Ibn Kathir's words, "to take the Children of Israel out of Egypt by night, and take them wherever he would be commanded." Two things are worth pausing over in that one sentence.

**The timing was part of the command.** They were not simply told to leave; they were told to leave by night. And they were not told where they were going — only that they were to be taken "wherever he would be commanded." They moved in the dark, under orders, without a stated destination.

**"My servants."** Notice whose they are. Allah calls them *ʿibādī*, "My servants." The contrast detonates two ayat later, when Fir'awn calls the very same people *shirdhima qalīlūn* — Ibn Kathir glosses it simply, "a small group." Allah names them by their relationship to Him; the tyrant names them by their headcount. That single difference is, in miniature, the whole passage.

**"You will indeed be pursued."** Allah tells Musa the chase is coming *before* it comes. This is not a warning that the plan might fail — the pursuit is announced by the One who is arranging the outcome, so that when the army appears behind them the believers will know they are still inside the command, not outside it.

## The night itself, in Ibn Kathir's reports

Ibn Kathir preserves several details of that night, and he is careful about how firmly he holds each one.

**The jewellery.** Musa (peace be upon him) "led them forth after they had borrowed an abundance of jewelry from the people of Fir'awn."

**The moon.** "As more than one of the scholars of Tafsir have said, they left when the moon was rising." Ibn Kathir then reports that Mujahid (may Allah have mercy on him) said the moon was eclipsed that night — and immediately follows it with "And Allah knows best," so the reader should hold that detail lightly, as he does.

**The remains of Yusuf.** In the middle of an evacuation, Musa (peace be upon him) asked about the grave of Yusuf (peace be upon him). An old woman from among the Children of Israel showed him where it was, and he took the remains with them. Ibn Kathir adds two further points as reports rather than settled fact: "it was said" they were among the things carried by Musa himself, and "it was said" that Yusuf (peace be upon him) had left instructions in his will that if the Children of Israel ever left Egypt, they should take his remains with them.

Still, the scene is worth sitting with. A whole people are leaving in the dark, a pursuit has already been announced, and the prophet stops to ask about one grave.

## Ayat 53–56 — the tyrant's speech

**Morning comes and the quarters are empty.** Ibn Kathir: "The following morning, when there was nobody to be found in the Israelite quarters, Fir'awn became angry and his anger intensified since Allah had decreed that he was to be destroyed." Read that causal clause slowly. The rage is not merely the reason he chased them; the intensifying of that rage is placed inside the decree against him. A man about to be destroyed is often destroyed *through* his own temper. Fir'awn thought he was reacting. He was being drawn.

**Ayah 53: the callers go out.** He "quickly sent his callers to all his cities" — Ibn Kathir explains the purpose: "to mobilize his troops and bring them together." An empire-wide muster.

**Ayah 54: "these indeed are but a small band."** Ibn Kathir glosses *shirdhima qalīlūn* as "a small group." But hear the propaganda in it. If they are so few, why summon every city? The boast and the mobilisation sit awkwardly together in adjacent ayat. This is how fear talks when it must not admit to being afraid: it belittles the thing it is arming against.

**Ayah 55: "they have done what has enraged us."** Ibn Kathir: "every time we have heard anything about them, it has upset us and made us angry." The grievance is chronic and unspecified — no crime is named, only an ongoing irritation. Tyranny is often at its angriest not when it is threatened but when it is disobeyed.

**Ayah 56: "we are all on the alert."** Ibn Kathir's first reading of *ḥādhirūn*: "we are constantly taking precautions lest they betray us." He then notes that some of the Salaf read it with the meaning "we are constantly forewarned and forearmed" — and, on that reading, the boast continues: "And I want to destroy them to the last man, and destroy all their lands and property."

Then Ibn Kathir delivers the verdict of the whole passage in one sentence: **"So he and his troops were punished with the very things he sought to inflict upon the Children of Israel."** Destroy them to the last man — he was destroyed to the last man. Take away their lands and property — his lands and property were taken away. The punishment was cut from the pattern of the crime.

## Ayat 57–58 — the tyrants brought out

*"So, We expelled them from gardens and springs, treasures, and every kind of honorable place."*

**Notice who the actor is.** Fir'awn thinks he is marching out to hunt. The Qur'an says: **We** expelled *them*. Every verb of consequence in this passage belongs to Allah — We revealed, We expelled, We caused to inherit. Fir'awn's only contribution is a speech.

**Notice the mirroring.** His stated aim, on the reading Ibn Kathir reports, was to destroy them to the last man and destroy their lands and property. It was his own people who were expelled from their gardens, springs, treasures and honourable places.

**What they lost.** Ibn Kathir reads it in two directions at once. Outwardly: "they left behind the honorable places, gardens and rivers, wealth, provision, position and power in this world." Finally: "they were thrown out of those blessings and into Hell." His phrasing keeps both losses in one breath, and that is the point: the man who leaves his garden to chase a people he called a small band ends up with neither the garden nor his soul.

*Maqām karīm* — an "honourable place" — covers more than architecture. Ibn Kathir's gloss includes "position and power." What Fir'awn lost was not only property; it was standing. And what it cost him was following his anger out of the palace gate.

## Ayah 59 — "So it was. And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them"

**"Thus" (kadhālika) — this is how Allah does it.** The ayah does not merely report an outcome; it labels it a pattern. Ibn Kathir places it alongside two other ayat that state the same law:

- *"And We made the people who were considered weak to inherit the eastern parts of the land and the western parts thereof which We have blessed"* (7:137).
- *"And We wished to do a favour to those who were weak in the land, and to make them rulers and to make them the inheritors"* (28:5–6).

Read together, these say something a persecuted believer needs to hear: being *considered weak* is not a verdict on your future. Allah's stated intention toward those who were weak in the land is favour, leadership and inheritance. Fir'awn counted them and called them few; Allah called them heirs.

## What exactly did they inherit? A real difficulty, honestly handled

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does not let this ayah pass without raising the obvious historical problem, and its treatment is a small lesson in scholarly honesty.

**The difficulty.** On the face of it, ayah 59 says the Children of Israel were made owners of the wealth and property left by Fir'awn's people after their drowning. But many Qur'anic verses indicate that they did not return to Egypt after that drowning. They went back instead toward their original home, the holy land of Syria (*al-Shām*). There they were commanded to fight a disbelieving nation in order to enter their city, refused, and as a punishment the open plain where they were camping became a natural prison: they could not leave it and spent forty years there. It was in that place — also known as the valley of Tīh (Sinai) — that their two prophets, Musa and Harun (peace be upon them), died. Nor is it reported in the books of history that the Children of Israel afterwards entered Egypt as a nation, collectively, in a way that would prove they took possession of the property of Fir'awn's people.

**Two answers, from two early authorities.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Tafsīr Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī preserves two explanations, from Hasan and from Qatadah (may Allah be pleased with them).

*Hasan's answer:* the ayah does mention that they were made heirs of the property of Fir'awn's people, but it does not say this happened immediately after Fir'awn's death. If they entered Egypt some forty or fifty years after the incident of the valley of Tīh, there is no inconsistency in the verse. As for the objection that their collective entry is not proved historically — that, on this view, is not worth taking notice of, because the history of that period was written by Jews and Christians and is full of distortions; there is no need to interpret a Qur'anic verse differently to bring it into line with a record whose own authenticity is questionable.

*Qatadah's answer:* the verses that recount this incident — 7:128 and 7:137, 28:5, 44:25–28, and this ayah of Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʼ — draw attention to the Children of Israel being given the very wealth and property Fir'awn's people had left in Egypt, which would have required their return. But all these verses can equally be read to mean that they were given wealth and property *equal and similar to* what Fir'awn's people had possessed, without it being the same lands. Those bounties may have been granted in Syria. Qatadah found this more likely in the wording of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, where the land they were given is called *"the land which We have blessed"* — because the word *bāraknā* is used for the land of Syria in many verses of the Qur'an. On this view it is not correct to read the verses in a way that conflicts with history.

**Where that leaves us.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up: if it is established through proved facts that the Children of Israel did not occupy the land of Egypt at any time after Fir'awn's death, then on Qatadah's explanation what was granted to them is the land of Syria. It closes, as the scholars do at such points, with *and Allah knows best*. Two respected readings; no manufactured certainty. That itself is worth learning from — a believer is allowed to hold a question open.

## Living it

**Obey the instruction you were given, not the one you wish you had.** Musa (peace be upon him) was told to move by night, told he would be pursued, and told he would be taken wherever he was commanded — not where that was. He went. Guidance often arrives like that: enough to take the next step, not enough to remove the fear.

**Being told the trouble is coming is a mercy.** "You will indeed be pursued" was said in advance, so that the pursuit, when it came, would not look like abandonment. Hardship that arrives inside Allah's stated plan is a different experience from hardship that seems to contradict it.

**Do not read your worth off the tyrant's headcount.** In one passage the same people are "My servants" and "a small band." One of those names is true.

**The plot returns to the plotter.** Ibn Kathir's line deserves memorising: he and his troops were punished with the very things he sought to inflict. What a person builds to crush others is very often the exact shape of what crushes him.

**Carry your trusts with you.** In the middle of the departure, Musa (peace be upon him) asked about the grave of Yusuf (peace be upon him) and took his remains along. Whatever else is left behind in a crisis, the trusts you are carrying travel with you.

passages.title: The sea parts and Pharaoh's host drowns
passages.tafsir:
These nine ayat carry the story of Musa (Moses) to its decisive moment. Ibn Kathir titles the passage: "Fir'awn's Pursuit and Expulsion of the Children of Israel, and How He and His People Were Drowned." The army overtakes the Children of Israel at the sea, Musa answers his people's panic with a single sentence of trust, the sea splits at Allah's command, the believers pass through, the pursuers are drowned — and ayat 67 and 68 tell us what the whole scene was for.

## The trap: ayat 60–61

Ibn Kathir reports that more than one of the scholars of tafsir said Fir'awn set out with a huge group — a group containing the leaders and entire government of Egypt at that time: the decision-makers and influential figures, princes, ministers, nobles, leaders and soldiers. This was not a raiding party. The full weight of a state was put behind one pursuit.

**"So they pursued them at sunrise" (ayah 60).** Ibn Kathir explains the phrase to mean that they caught up with the Children of Israel at sunrise. There is something merciless in that timing. The night's head start is over, and the light comes up on exactly what is behind you.

**"And when the two hosts saw each other" (ayah 61).** Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: each group saw the other. Not a scout's report and not a rumour — two masses of people looking straight at one another.

Then the geometry of the trap, as Ibn Kathir sets it out: Fir'awn and his people caught up with them on the shores of the Red Sea, so the sea was ahead of them and Fir'awn and his troops were behind them. Hemmed between water and swords, the people said, **"innā la-mudrakūn"** — "We are sure to be overtaken." Ma'arif ul Quran puts the scene plainly: when the pursuing army reached right behind them, all the people of Bani Isra'il called out that they were caught — and there was little doubt about it, with the water in front of them and the enormous army behind.

**Where each person stood.** Ibn Kathir preserves the arrangement of the column: Harun, peace be upon him, was in the front, with Yusha' bin Nun and a believer from the family of Fir'awn; Musa, peace be upon him, was in the rear. The prophet placed himself on the side the danger was coming from.

He also records that they stood there not knowing what to do, and that Yusha' bin Nun — or the believer from the family of Fir'awn — said to Musa, peace be upon him, "O Prophet of Allah, is it here that your Lord commanded you to bring us?" He said: "Yes." Then Fir'awn and his troops drew near, and were very close indeed.

That question is worth sitting with. It is not mockery; it is a believer double-checking the one thing that still matters when everything visible has gone wrong: *are we where Allah told us to be?* Once the answer is yes, the rest of the situation, however hopeless it looks, is Allah's affair.

## The sentence at the centre: ayah 62

**"Kallā! Inna ma'iya rabbī sa-yahdīn"** — "Nay! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me."

Musa does not soften their fear; he contradicts it. Ibn Kathir gives the sense of his answer: nothing of what you fear will happen to you, for Allah is the One Who commanded me to bring you here, and He does not go back on His promise. Ma'arif ul Quran describes the same moment from Musa's side: he was fully aware of the situation, but his belief in the promise of Allah was unshaken like a rock, and so he replied firmly that they would never be caught.

Look at how the reply is built. Musa does not say "there is a way out" — he has no route to point to. He says two things only: **my Lord is with me**, and **He will guide me**. Guidance has not arrived yet; he is standing in front of water with an army closing behind him and has been given no instructions. His certainty is not certainty about the plan; it is certainty about the One who has the plan. Ma'arif ul Quran observes that such are the moments in which faith is tested, and that Musa, peace be upon him, was not terror-stricken at all — it was as if he could see the way out for himself.

## The cave of Thaur: a parallel worth knowing

Ma'arif ul Quran draws a striking comparison. Almost the same thing happened to the Prophet ﷺ at the time of the migration, while he was hiding in the cave of Thaur. The enemy in pursuit had reached right at the opening of the cave — so close that they could have seen him had they looked down towards their toes. Sayyidna Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) became a little alarmed, and the Prophet ﷺ said exactly the same thing that Musa had said: **"Lā taḥzan, inna Allāha ma'anā"** — "Do not grieve; Allah is surely with us" (9:40).

Then comes the fine observation. Musa, peace be upon him, consoling his ummah, said *ma'iya rabbī* — "with **me** is my Lord." The Prophet ﷺ, replying to Abu Bakr, said *ma'anā* — "Allah is with **us** (two)." Ma'arif ul Quran draws from this a special privilege of the ummah of Muhammad ﷺ: that his followers too are honoured by the company of Allah when they are with their Messenger ﷺ.

For a believer reading this, the two scenes teach the same discipline: when you are where obedience placed you, the arithmetic of the situation stops being the point.

## The sea splits: ayah 63

"So We revealed to Musa: 'Strike the sea with your staff.'"

Ibn Kathir marks the timing exactly: it was at that point — after the standing still, after the question, after Fir'awn and his troops had drawn very close indeed — that Allah commanded His Prophet Musa, peace be upon him, to strike the sea with his staff; so he struck it, and it parted, by the will of Allah.

Two things are worth noticing. First, the command came late, not early. Musa's confidence in ayah 62 was spoken *before* he knew what would happen. Second, the instruction, when it came, was almost absurdly small: strike water with a stick. The staff did not split the sea. Ibn Kathir's phrase is careful: it parted **by the will of Allah**. What is asked of the servant is the action, however slight; the outcome belongs entirely to Allah.

**"Fa-nfalaqa fa-kāna kullu firqin ka-l-ṭawdi l-'aẓīm"** — "and it parted, and each separate part became like a huge mountain." Ibn Kathir explains the comparison as meaning *like mighty mountains*, and records this as the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad bin Ka'b, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah and others. 'Ata' Al-Khurasani understood it differently: "It refers to a pass between two mountains."

Ibn Kathir then gathers what the early authorities transmitted about the scene:

- **Ibn 'Abbas:** "The sea divided into twelve paths, one for each of the tribes."
- **As-Suddi:** "And in it there were windows through which they could see one another, and the water was erected like walls."
- And Allah sent the wind to the sea bed to make it solid like the land — as He says elsewhere, *"and strike a dry path for them in the sea, fearing neither to be overtaken nor being afraid"* (20:77).

Notice how closely that verse of Surah Ta-Ha answers what the people had just said. They cried *innā la-mudrakūn* — "we are sure to be overtaken"; and Allah's word to Musa is *lā takhāfu darakan* — "fearing neither to be overtaken." Their dread is named, and cancelled.

## "And We brought the others near": ayah 64

*Wa azlafnā thamma l-ākharīn.* Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' Al-Khurasani, Qatadah and As-Suddi that *azlafnā* means: "We brought Fir'awn and his troops near to the sea."

This is one of the quietest and most frightening statements in the passage. Fir'awn believed he was the one doing the chasing. In the Qur'an's own telling, he was being **brought** — drawn near to the sea by Allah. A ruler at the height of his power, with his whole government behind him, moving with total confidence, and the movement itself belongs to the One he denied.

## Rescue and ruin: ayat 65–66

"And We saved Musa and all those with him. Then We drowned the others."

Ibn Kathir's comment brings out how complete each half is: We saved Musa and the Children of Israel and whoever followed their religion, and **none of them** were destroyed; but Fir'awn and his troops were drowned, and not one of them remained alive.

The wording of ayah 65 underlines it — "all together." Salvation with no casualties; destruction with no survivors. There was no middle outcome, and the line between the two groups was not strength or numbers: it ran between those with Musa, and whoever followed the religion he brought, on one side, and Fir'awn's host on the other.

Notice also the verbs across this sequence. The acting subject is Allah: *We revealed*, *We brought near*, *We saved*, *We drowned*. Musa struck; Allah did everything else.

## The refrain: ayat 67–68

"Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord — He is truly the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful."

**"Indeed in that is a sign."** Ibn Kathir explains: this story, with its wonders and its tales of aid to the believing servants of Allah, is definitive proof and evidence of Allah's wisdom. The sign is not only the parting of the water; it is the pattern the whole account displays — that Allah aids those who believe in Him.

**"Yet most of them were not believers."** This is the sober note that keeps the passage from being a mere adventure. Such things were witnessed, and still most did not come to faith. What the eye sees does not by itself settle what the heart accepts.

**"And indeed your Lord — He is truly al-'Azīz, ar-Raḥīm."** The scene closes by naming the Lord with two of His names: the All-Mighty and the Most Merciful. Ibn Kathir does not comment on the phrase here, noting only that its explanation has already been discussed earlier in his tafsir — so this material offers no exposition of the two names, and none should be manufactured. What the passage itself sets before us is the naming: after all that has been recounted, the last word is about who your Lord is.

## Living it

**Ask the question Yusha' asked.** When a situation closes in, the first thing to settle is not "how do I escape?" but "am I where obedience put me?" If the answer is yes, then what Ibn Kathir says of Musa's confidence applies: Allah is the One Who commanded this, and He does not go back on His promise.

**Say Musa's sentence before you can see the way out.** *Inna ma'iya rabbī sa-yahdīn* is spoken with the water in front and the army behind. Ma'arif ul Quran calls such moments the test of faith. Trust that waits for a visible exit has not yet been tested.

**Strike the sea.** The command was small and the result was beyond all proportion to it, and Ibn Kathir attributes the parting not to the staff but to the will of Allah. Do the little that is asked of you — the phone call, the repentance, the honest word — and leave the parting of the water to Allah.

**Stay with the Messenger ﷺ.** Ma'arif ul Quran's observation on *ma'anā* is an encouragement worth carrying: the followers of the Prophet ﷺ are honoured by the company of Allah when they are with their Messenger ﷺ. Nearness to what he brought is not a small thing; it is the side of the line you want to be standing on.

passages.title: Abraham questions his people about their idols
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are a single conversation — a short, searching cross-examination that Ibrahim, upon him be peace, conducts with his own father and his own people about the idols they worship. What holds ayat 69–76 together is that they form one unbroken exchange: Allah commands His Prophet ﷺ to recite the story (69), Ibrahim asks his opening question (70), his people answer (71), he presses them with three test questions (72–73), they retreat to the practice of their ancestors (74), and he turns that answer back on them (75–76).

## "And recite to them" — why this story, and why now

Ayah 69 is addressed not to Ibrahim but to Muhammad ﷺ: *And recite to them the story of Ibrahim.* Ibn Kathir explains that Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to recite this story to his Ummah **so that they could follow this example** — the example of sincerity towards Allah, of putting one's trust in Him, of worshipping Him alone with no partner or associate, and of renouncing shirk and the people of shirk. (*Shirk* means associating partners with Allah in worship — giving to something other than Him what belongs to Him alone.)

That single sentence tells you how to read everything that follows. This is not merely a historical anecdote about ancient statues. It is a model handed to a community, so that they might live by what Ibrahim lived by.

Ibn Kathir introduces Ibrahim here with three titles: Allah's **servant**, His **Messenger**, and His **Close Friend**, and calls him "the leader of the pure monotheists." He also notes that Allah granted Ibrahim guidance beforehand — that is, from a very early age he had denounced his people's practice of worshipping idols alongside Allah. So the confidence in these ayat is not that of a man who stumbled onto the truth late. It is the clarity of someone Allah had guided from the start.

## The opening question (ayah 70)

Ibrahim does not begin with a sermon, a threat, or a verdict. He begins with a question: **مَا تَعْبُدُونَ** — *"What do you worship?"*

Two things are worth noticing. First, he addresses **"his father and his people"** together. The hardest listener and the wider audience in one breath. He does not exempt his own household from the question he puts to the town, and he does not soften it because the first man listening is his father.

Second, Ibn Kathir's gloss captures the force of the question: *"what are these statues to which you are so devoted?"* It is designed to make them look at the object itself. Not at the ritual, not at the feeling, not at the custom — at the carved thing. Almost every false belief survives by never being asked to describe itself plainly. Ibrahim makes them describe it.

## Their answer (ayah 71)

**نَعْبُدُ أَصْنَامًا فَنَظَلُّ لَهَا عَاكِفِينَ** — *"We worship idols, to which we are fully devoted."*

They answer honestly, and in answering they hand him the case. They do not say "we worship the Creator through these." They name the object plainly: idols, statues. And then they add the intensity of their commitment — rendered as *"ever devoted"* and *"fully devoted."* Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as: *we are devoted to worshipping them and praying to them.*

That is the whole problem in miniature. They describe the *degree* of their devotion as though degree were the argument: how constant they are, how attached, how immovable. Sincerity of feeling is offered in place of any account of the object. It is a mistake people still make — "look how deeply I believe this" is not an answer to "is this true?"

## The three questions (ayat 72–73)

Now Ibrahim applies the test, and it is beautifully economical — three questions, and if the answer to all three is no, the case is closed:

1. **هَلْ يَسْمَعُونَكُمْ إِذْ تَدْعُونَ** — *"Can they hear you when you call upon them?"* (72)
2. **أَوْ يَنفَعُونَكُمْ** — *"Or can they benefit you…"* (73)
3. **أَوْ يَضُرُّونَ** — *"…or harm you?"* (73)

Notice what he asks about first: **hearing**. Not power, not knowledge, not creation — hearing. Because worship as they themselves had just described it involved *praying to them*, calling upon them. So Ibrahim goes straight to the hinge of that act: when you speak, is anyone there? If the thing you address cannot receive your address, the entire practice is a man speaking into an empty room.

Then benefit and harm — the two motives that hold a person to any object of worship. You cling to something because you hope for good from it or fear evil from it. Ibrahim removes both. Nothing to gain, nothing to fear.

And here Ibn Kathir makes the most piercing observation in the whole passage: **"They knew that their idols could not do anything."** They were not deceived. There was no confusion to clear up. They were aware their statues heard nothing and did nothing — and they went on anyway. Which is why the answer in ayah 74 is what it is.

## The answer that is not an answer (ayah 74)

**بَلْ وَجَدْنَا آبَاءَنَا كَذَٰلِكَ يَفْعَلُونَ** — *"No! But we found our forefathers doing the same."*

Read it as a piece of conversation and it is remarkable. He asked three factual questions. They answered none of them. They do not claim the idols hear, or benefit, or harm. They change the subject to their fathers.

Ibn Kathir puts it exactly: they knew the idols could do nothing, "but they had seen their fathers doing this, so they made haste to follow in their footsteps." They abandon the claim and keep the practice.

This is the moment the passage is really about. The idolatry in front of us is not an intellectual error that better information would fix — Ibn Kathir has just told us they already had the information. It is a loyalty: to family, to continuity, to the comfort of not being the one who breaks the chain. That is why Ibrahim's next move is not to supply more facts.

## "Do you observe…" (ayat 75–76)

Ibn Kathir renders Ibrahim's reply: *"Do you observe that which you have been worshipping – you and your ancient fathers?"*

It is the question of ayah 70 asked again — but now with everything they have just admitted attached to it, and with one change. Instead of arguing against the ancestors, Ibrahim **widens the question to include them**. They had said "we found our forefathers doing the same," hoping the weight of the past would settle the matter. He answers, in effect: then look at what they were worshipping too. *You and your ancestors.*

If the test of hearing, benefit and harm has just failed in front of them today, it failed in their fathers' hands as well. Age does not make a false thing true; it only tells you how long the practice has been running. And Ibn Kathir carries this sentence straight on into what Ibrahim says next in the following ayah — that these idols are enemies to him, save the Lord of all the worlds.

## Living it

Ibn Kathir has already told us why this story was recited: so that the Ummah would **follow this example** — sincerity towards Allah, trust in Him, worshipping Him alone with no partner, and renouncing shirk and its people. Concretely, that asks a few things of us.

**Look plainly at what you serve.** Ibrahim's opening move was to make people name the object of their devotion and look at it. That question can be turned inward without any drama: what am I actually serving, and what is it in itself?

**Test; do not simply feel.** The people's first answer was about the intensity of their attachment; Ibrahim's reply was about the capacity of the object. Depth of feeling establishes nothing about the worth of what is felt for. Allah alone hears the one who calls upon Him; benefit and harm are in His hand alone.

**Do not let "we found our fathers doing so" be your reason.** Ibn Kathir's diagnosis is that they hurried after their fathers' footsteps while knowing better. Inherited practice, however old and however beloved, is not evidence.

**Be willing to be the one who breaks the chain.** Ibrahim asks his question of his own father first, and of his whole town in the same breath. Renouncing shirk and its people — which is precisely what Ibn Kathir says this story was given to us to imitate — is not a private opinion quietly held. It cost Ibrahim the ease of belonging, and he paid it while standing in front of the people he loved most.

passages.title: "They are all my enemies, except the Lord of all worlds"
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the turning point of Ibrahim's argument with his father and his people. Having pressed them on whether their idols can hear, benefit or harm, he now does two things in one breath: he cuts himself off from those idols entirely (ayah 77), and then he describes, in five statements, the One he *does* worship — the Lord who made him, guides him, feeds him, heals him, will take his life and raise him, and whose forgiveness he hopes for (ayat 78–82). The rejection is not merely negative; it immediately becomes a portrait of Allah drawn from Ibrahim's own life, from his creation to his standing on the Day of Recompense.

## Where we are in the story

Ibn Kathir sets the scene from the ayat just before. Allah, he says, is telling us about "His servant, Messenger and Close Friend, Ibrahim, upon him be peace, the leader of the pure monotheists" — and Allah commanded His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ to recite this story to his Ummah so that they could follow this example of sincerity towards Allah, putting one's trust in Him, worshipping Him alone with no partner or associate, and renouncing shirk and its people. Ibn Kathir adds that Allah granted guidance to Ibrahim early: from a very young age he had denounced his people's practice of worshipping idols alongside Allah.

Ibrahim had begun with a question (ayah 70): *"What do you worship?"* — which Ibn Kathir paraphrases as, what are these statues to which you are so devoted? They answered that they worshipped idols and were "ever devoted" to them, meaning, in Ibn Kathir's words, devoted to worshipping them and praying to them. So Ibrahim pressed with the only questions that matter about an object of worship (ayat 72–73): *Do they hear you when you call? Or do they benefit you or do they cause harm?*

Their answer was not an answer. *"We found our fathers doing so."* Ibn Kathir's comment here is quietly devastating: **they knew that their idols could not do anything** — but they had seen their fathers doing this, so they made haste to follow in their footsteps. Inherited practice was doing the work that evidence could not do. Ibrahim then asks them to *look* at it (ayat 75–76): "Do you observe that which you have been worshipping — you and your ancient fathers?" And then comes ayah 77.

## Ayah 77: a declaration of open enmity

*"They are all enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds."*

Notice who is speaking and about what. Ibrahim has just named "that which you have been worshipping — you and your ancient fathers," and now says of those objects: they are my enemies. The break is with the idols themselves, and the exception carved out is not a person or a tribe but "the Lord of all worlds" — *Rabb al-ʿālamīn* — the only One left standing once everything else has been declared hostile.

Ibn Kathir reads the statement as a challenge thrown down in the open. Its meaning, he says, is: *"if these idols mean anything and have any influence, then let them do me any kind of harm, for I am an enemy to them and I do not care about them or think anything of them."* That is worth pausing over. The words as they stand say "they are enemies to me"; Ibn Kathir's gloss turns the sentence around to show what Ibrahim is really doing — he is not complaining of persecution by stones, he is **declaring himself their enemy** and daring them to retaliate. A man who says that to the gods of a whole city is either mad or absolutely certain.

**The pattern of the Messengers.** Ibn Kathir shows that this defiance is not Ibrahim's alone; it is how Allah's Messengers speak. Allah described Nuh saying, *"So devise your plot, you and your partners"* (10:71). Hud, upon him be peace, said, *"I call Allah to witness and bear you witness that I am free from that which you ascribe as partners in worship. So plot against me, all of you, and give me no respite. I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord! There is not a moving creature but He has the grasp of its forelock. Verily, my Lord is on the straight path"* (11:54–56). And Ibrahim himself, denouncing their gods and idols, said elsewhere, *"And how should I fear those whom you associate in worship with Allah, while you fear not that you have joined in worship with Allah"* (6:81). The logic in every case is the same: the man who fears Allah alone has nothing left to fear, while the one who fears creation has neglected the only fear that was ever warranted.

**Why this is preserved for us.** Ibn Kathir cites Allah's own verdict on this scene: *"Indeed there has been an excellent example for you in Ibrahim"* — running on to *"until you believe in Allah alone"* (60:4). And he brings the parallel from Sūrah al-Zukhruf, where Ibrahim says to his father and his people, *"Verily, I am innocent of what you worship, except Him Who created me; and verily, He will guide me,"* and Allah adds, *"And he made it a Word lasting among his offspring, that they may turn back"* (43:26–28). That lasting word, Ibn Kathir says, is **"La Ilaha Illallah"** — there is no god but Allah. The sentence Ibrahim spoke did not die with him; Allah made it endure in his descendants as the thing they could always return to.

## Ayat 78–82: the One worth worshipping, described from a life

Ibn Kathir titles this section *"Ibrahim Mentions Allah's Kindness Towards Him"*, and summarises Ibrahim's stance in a single sentence: **"I will not worship any but the One Who does these things."** Ibrahim does not argue abstractly. He points at his own existence, item by item, and asks in effect: which of these did a statue ever do for you?

**"Who has created me, and it is He Who guides me"** (ayah 78). Ibn Kathir joins the two halves rather than separating them: He is the Creator who has decreed certain things to which He guides His creation, so each person follows the path which is decreed for him — and Allah is the One who guides whomsoever He wills and leaves astray whomsoever He wills. So guidance is not an afterthought bolted onto creation; it belongs to the same Lordship. The One who made you is the only one qualified to tell you what you are for.

**"And it is He Who feeds me and gives me to drink"** (ayah 79). Ibn Kathir expands the everyday miracle behind the words: He is my Creator who provides for me from that which He has made available in the heavens and on earth; He drives the clouds and causes water to fall, with which He revives the earth and brings forth its fruits as provision for mankind; He sends down the water fresh and sweet so that many of those He has created, animals and men alike, may drink from it. Your lunch has a supply chain that runs back through cloud and rain and the reviving of dead soil, and no idol appears anywhere on it.

**"And when I am ill, it is He Who cures me"** (ayah 80). This is the most delicate line in the passage, and Ibn Kathir's remark on it is one of the great observations in tafsir. Ibrahim says "when *I* am ill" — **here he attributed sickness to himself, even though it is Allah who decrees it, out of respect towards Allah.** Everything pleasant in the list is said plainly of Allah: He created, He guides, He feeds, He gives drink, He cures. The illness alone is left in the first person.

Ibn Kathir shows that the Qur'an teaches us this same manner of speech elsewhere. By the same token, he says, Allah commands us to say in the prayer, *"Guide us to the straight way"* (1:6) and on to the end of the Sūrah: grace and guidance are attributed to Allah, may He be exalted, but the subject of the verb with reference to anger is omitted, and going astray is attributed to the people. He gives a further example from the words of the jinn: *"And we know not whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them a right path"* (72:10) — again, the good is named to their Lord, and the harm is left unattributed.

Understand what this does and does not mean. It is not a denial that illness comes about by Allah's decree — Ibn Kathir states outright that it is Allah who decrees it. It is a lesson in how a servant *speaks* about his Lord: the tongue leans towards mentioning Him in connection with mercy. As for the cure itself, Ibn Kathir's meaning of the ayah is: *"when I fall sick, no one is able to heal me but Him, Who heals me with the means that may lead to recovery."* That last phrase is important and balanced — the healing is Allah's alone, and He works it **through means**. Seeking treatment is not a rival to trusting Allah; the medicine is one of His instruments, and the cure is still from Him.

**"And Who will cause me to die, and then will bring me to life"** (ayah 81). He is the One who gives life and causes death, says Ibn Kathir, and no one besides Him is able to do that, for He is the One who originates and repeats. The same power that started you can start you again — which is why the resurrection is not a strange claim but the sequel to the first creation.

**"And Who, I hope, will forgive me my faults on the Day of Recompense"** (ayah 82). Ibn Kathir: this means that no one is able to forgive sins in this world or the Hereafter except Him. *Who can forgive sins except Allah?* For He is the One who does whatever He wills.

## The shape of the list — and where it ends

Read ayat 78–82 in order and you see a life laid end to end: brought into being, guided, fed, healed when broken, taken in death, raised again, and finally standing before Allah in need of pardon. One Lord is behind every stage of it, and the idols are absent from all of them.

Then look at how the confidence changes at the last step. The earlier statements are flat and certain: He created, He guides, He feeds, He cures, He will cause me to die and bring me to life. Only in ayah 82 does Ibrahim say *"I hope"* — *aṭmaʿu*. Ibrahim, the Close Friend of Allah and the leader of the pure monotheists, does not say "and He will forgive me." As Ibn Kathir puts it, no one can forgive sins except Allah, for He is the One who does whatever He wills; forgiveness is His to give, not anyone's to claim. So the man who a moment earlier stared down a city's gods speaks of his own faults with lowered eyes. Two attitudes in the same speech, and both are faith: absolute fearlessness before creation, absolute humility before the Creator.

## "Indeed, with me is my Lord"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, commenting in this part of the Sūrah, shows what such certainty about guidance looks like under pressure. It takes up the words of Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) earlier in this same Sūrah — *"Indeed with me is my Lord. He will guide me"* (26:62) — and notes that such are the moments for the test of faith, yet Musa was not terror-stricken at all, as if he was seeing for himself the way out.

Almost the same thing happened, the commentary continues, with the Holy Prophet ﷺ at the time of the migration, while hiding in the cave of Thaur. The enemy had reached right at the opening of the cave in pursuit — so close that they could have seen him if they had looked down towards their toes. Sayyidna Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, got alarmed a little, but the Prophet ﷺ said exactly the same kind of thing: *"Do not grieve, Allah is surely with us"* (9:40).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to one difference between the two incidents. Musa said, to console his people, *"With me is my Lord"*; the Prophet ﷺ said to Abu Bakr, *"Allah is with **us** (the two of us)."* It is a special privilege of the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, the commentary says, that his followers are also honoured by the company of Allah when they are with their Messenger.

This is the same conviction Ibrahim voices in ayah 78 — *He created me, and He guides me* — held onto when the outward situation looks hopeless and the inward one is settled.

## Living it

- **Test what you rely on by Ibrahim's two questions** (ayat 72–73): does it hear you when you call, and can it actually benefit or harm you? Idols today are rarely carved, but anything you fear or hope in as though it controlled your provision, health or future is being asked those questions.
- **Beware the answer they gave.** "We found our fathers doing so" is the reasoning of people who, as Ibn Kathir says, *knew* their idols could not do anything and followed the practice anyway. Inherited custom is not evidence, and habit is not proof.
- **Learn Ibrahim's manner of speech** from ayah 80: when hardship comes, be careful how you phrase it — the fault and the going astray are ours; the guidance, the healing and the mercy are His.
- **Take the means and trust the Healer.** Ibn Kathir's wording is the balance: He heals "with the means that may lead to recovery." See the doctor; know who cures.
- **Recount the list when your faith feels thin.** Ibrahim argued for tawhid by naming what Allah had done for him personally. That argument is available to you every day, and it ends where his ends — in hope for forgiveness on the Day of Recompense.

passages.title: Abraham's prayer for wisdom and a pure heart
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat are a single supplication. Ibn Kathir titles the passage "The Prayer of Ibrahim for Himself and for His Father." What holds it together is its movement: it begins with what he wants to *be* in this world, rises to what he wants to *leave behind*, then to what he wants to *receive* in the Hereafter, then turns outward to his father — and that turn opens onto the Day of Resurrection itself, so that the du'a ends not with a request at all but with a verdict on what will actually count on that Day: a sound heart.

## The shape of the asking (ayat 83–85)

**"My Lord! Grant me wisdom."** The Arabic word is *ḥukm*. Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn 'Abbas explained it here as **knowledge**. It is the first thing Ibrahim asks for — before remembrance among people, before Paradise itself. The order of the requests is itself instruction.

**"And join me with the righteous."** Ibn Kathir explains this as: *make me one of the righteous in this world and the Hereafter.* He sets beside it, as a comparable prayer, the words the Prophet ﷺ said three times when he was dying: **"O Allah, with the Exalted Companion (of Paradise)."** Ibn Kathir offers this as a likeness — one supplication illuminating another — and the likeness is worth sitting with: the last words are not a request for a rank, but to be with.

**"And bless me with honourable mention among later generations" (84).** The Arabic is *lisān ṣidq*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *lisān* — which literally means "tongue" — is used here in the sense of **description**, and "for me" means "for my benefit." So the meaning of the prayer is: *O Allah, grant me such fine ways and good marks that others may follow them until the Day of Judgement, and remember me with good words and fine attributes* (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn Kathir and Rūḥ al-Maʿānī). Ibn Kathir puts it as: *cause me to be remembered in a good manner after my death, so that I will be spoken of and taken as a good example* — and he points to Allah's own answer to this prayer elsewhere in the Qur'an: "And We left for him a goodly remembrance among the later generations: 'Peace be upon Ibrahim. Thus indeed do We reward the good doers'" (37:108–110).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes how completely that prayer was answered: Jews, Christians, and even the disbelievers of Makkah have feelings of love and affection for the creed of Ibrahim and attribute themselves to it — though their ways, built on disbelief and polytheism, are in conflict with his. It is the Ummah of the Prophet ﷺ who rightly claim to be on the ways of Ibrahim.

**"And make me one of those awarded the Garden of Bliss" (85).** Ibn Kathir joins 84 and 85 into one sweep: *bless me in this world with honourable mention after I am gone, and in the Hereafter by making me one of the inheritors of the Paradise of Delight.* The whole prayer, then, spans both abodes in a single breath — the trace left behind here, and the dwelling received there.

## Is it permitted to want to be well thought of?

Ayah 84 raises a real difficulty, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān faces it squarely. Love and aspiration for being praised and respected by others is contemptible under Islamic law. The Qur'an has made the bounties of the Hereafter dependent on desisting from that love: "As for that Ultimate Abode, We assign it to those who intend neither being high on earth nor mischief" (28:83). So how does a prophet pray for his own good name?

Maʿārif's answer is that a careful look at the wording of the ayah shows the difference. Ibrahim is not asking to be admired; the real purpose of the supplication was to invoke divine help for performing such righteous deeds as would help him in the Hereafter — and that others, including the generations to come, be drawn towards those righteous deeds by following his example. What the Qur'an and hadith condemn under "love of praise" is love of **worldly position of importance and profit**, and that is simply not what is in this prayer.

The warnings are severe. Imam Tirmidhi and Nasa'i relate on the authority of Ka'b ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: **if two hungry wolves are let loose in a herd of goats, they would not do as much damage to the herd as two traits do to a man's faith — the love of wealth, and the aspiration to be praised and respected.** (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Ṭabarānī relates it from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and Bazzār from Abu Hurayrah.) Dailamī reproduces a narration on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas — **with a weak chain of narrators**, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to state — that love of praise and worldly status makes a man blind and deaf.

But all of these, Maʿārif explains, refer to the love that has worldly considerations, or for which one has to indulge in sin or negligence in the matter of faith. Where that is absent, aspiration for praise and high position is not contemptible. A supplication is reported from the Prophet ﷺ himself: *"O Allah, make me insignificant in my own sight, but make me great in the eyes of people"* — and there too, Maʿārif explains, the purpose of being great in people's eyes is that people emulate him in his righteous deeds. (The source reports this supplication without naming a collection, so it is given here as the commentator transmits it, not as a graded narration.)

The scholars then drew the line precisely:

- **Imam Malik** said that one who is in fact virtuous and pious is required only to avoid making deliberate efforts to present himself as pious in the eyes of people; otherwise, if he loves to be praised by people, that is not contemptible.
- **Ibn 'Arabi** said it is evident from this ayah that *desiring a righteous deed which results in people's praise* is allowed.
- **Imam Ghazali** ruled that love of praise and a position of respect is permissible under three conditions: (1) the object is not to proclaim oneself superior to others and degrade them, but benefit in the Hereafter, so that others may be influenced to follow his example; (2) the object is not to earn praise for a trait one does not possess; (3) achieving it does not require indulging in sin or negligence in the matter of faith.

## "And forgive my father" (86)

This is the hardest line in the passage, and both commentaries treat it as a genuine problem to be solved rather than passed over.

The difficulty: the Qur'an states plainly, "It is not for the Prophet and the believers to seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they are kinsmen, after it became clear to them that they are the people of hell" (9:113). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the rule from it directly — **it is not allowed for a Muslim to pray for the forgiveness of someone about whom it is certainly known that he died in the state of disbelief.** So how did Ibrahim pray for a father who was a disbeliever?

Maʿārif answers that Allah Himself has given the answer in the Qur'an: "And the prayer of Ibrahim for the forgiveness of his father was not but due to a promise he had made to him. Later, when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he withdrew himself from him. Surely Ibrahim is *awwāh* — oft-sighing before Allah — and forbearing" (9:114).

The gist of the answer, Maʿārif says, is one of two things: either Ibrahim supplicated for his father's pardon **within his father's lifetime**, with the intent and desire that Allah would give him the divine help to turn to faith — after which forgiveness was sure; or Ibrahim was of the opinion that his father had accepted faith but had not made it public. Once he learnt that his father had died in disbelief, he pronounced himself free of him. (Maʿārif adds a note: whether Ibrahim became aware of his father's disbelief within his own lifetime, or after his father's death, or would know it only on the Day of Judgement, is discussed fully under Surah at-Tawbah.)

Ibn Kathir traces the same arc through the Qur'an: this prayer is like the ayah "My Lord! Forgive me, and my parents" (71:28) — but it is **something Ibrahim later stopped doing**, and Allah stopped him from asking forgiveness for his father, as in 60:4, where Ibrahim and those with him are called an excellent example, and where he says, "I have no power to do anything for you before Allah."

What follows for the reader is the boundary Maʿārif draws: the du'a Ibrahim made was made in hope for a man still living. Once death upon disbelief is certain, that du'a is no longer ours to make — and the Qur'an, in the very ayah that records Ibrahim withdrawing, still describes him as tender and forbearing.

## "And do not disgrace me on the Day all will be resurrected" (87)

Ibn Kathir explains: *protect me from shame on the Day of Resurrection, the Day when all creatures, the first and the last, will be raised.* Note what a prophet fears — not punishment first, but **disgrace**, being exposed before all creation.

Al-Bukhari recorded that Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said that the Prophet ﷺ said: **"Ibrahim will see his father on the Day of Resurrection, covered with dust and darkness."** According to another narration, also from Abu Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said that Ibrahim will meet his father and say, "O Lord, You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the Day when all creatures are resurrected" — and Allah will say to him, **"I have forbidden Paradise to the disbelievers."** Al-Bukhari also recorded it among the accounts of the Prophets, upon them be peace, with fuller wording: Ibrahim will meet his father Azar on the Day of Resurrection, and there will be dust and darkness on Azar's face. Ibrahim will say to him, "Did I not tell you not to disobey me?" His father will say, "Today I will not disobey you." Ibrahim will say, "O Lord, You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the Day when they are resurrected — but what disgrace can be greater than seeing my father in this state?" Allah will say, "I have forbidden Paradise to the disbelievers." Then it will be said, "O Ibrahim! Look beneath your feet." He will look, and there he will see that his father was changed into **a male hyena covered in dung**, which will be caught by the legs and thrown into the Fire. This was also recorded by Abu 'Abdur-Rahman An-Nasa'i in the Tafsir of his Sunan al-Kubra.

The narration is severe, and it is meant to be. Allah's own words within it settle the matter: Paradise is forbidden to the disbelievers. Even a prophet's plea, and even the closest tie of blood, does not move that line.

## "The Day when neither wealth nor children will be of any benefit" (88)

Ibn Kathir explains it as ransom: a man's wealth will not protect him from the punishment of Allah, **even if he were to pay a ransom equivalent to an earthful of gold**; and "nor sons" means — or if he were to pay a ransom of all the people on earth. On that Day nothing will be of any avail except faith in Allah and sincere devotion to Him, and renunciation of shirk and its people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the word *banūn* — literally restricted to **male children**. The reason, Maʿārif suggests, is probably that it is male children from whom effective help is expected in adverse situations; even in this world, expecting help from daughters in a calamity is very rare. So the male children are named specifically in the context of the Hereafter to indicate that **even those who were expected to help in this world will be of no use there.**

## "Except those who come to Allah with a sound heart" (89)

**The grammar first.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that this exception, *illā*, has been interpreted in two ways:

- Some commentators read it as *munqaṭiʿ* — an exception of a special type that does not exclude anything from the preceding statement, but simply says that the thing negated in the first sentence is found in someone else. Maʿārif gives a simple example: a person is asked about Zayd, whether he has wealth and children, and replies, "No — his wealth and children are nothing but his sound heart." On this reading, wealth and children will not be helpful to anyone, believer or disbeliever; what will be helpful instead is one's sound heart, that is, true faith and righteous deeds.
- **The majority** read it as a normal exception: wealth and children *may* be helpful to the one who comes to Allah with a sound heart — with faith and righteous deeds — but will be of no use to a disbeliever.

**Then the word itself.** Maʿārif notes that "sound heart" **literally means a healthy heart**. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as a heart free from any impurity or shirk. The early authorities gave complementary descriptions:

- **Ibn 'Abbas** — here it means the heart of a believer, which testifies to the Oneness of Allah and is pure of shirk. Maʿārif reports the same interpretation, in different expressions, from **Mujahid**, **Hasan al-Basri**, and **Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab**.
- **Ibn Sirin** — "The clean heart knows that Allah is true, that the Hour will undoubtedly come, and that Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves."
- **Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab** — "The clean heart is the sound heart," that is, the heart of the believer; the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite is sick, as Allah says: "In their hearts is a disease" (2:10).
- **Abu 'Uthman an-Nisaburi** — "It is the heart that is free from innovation and is content with the Sunnah."

Read together they give the picture: right belief about Allah, certainty about the Hour and the Resurrection, no partner set up beside Allah, and contentment with the Sunnah rather than with what has been added to it.

## Wealth and family after all — on the majority's reading

Because the commonly adopted explanation takes the exception in ayah 89 as a real one, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out what that means practically. A person's wealth **can** be of help to him on that Day — provided he is a Muslim. Whatever he spent in this world in the way of Allah and in the cause of righteous deeds, or in ongoing charity (*ṣadaqah jāriyah*), he will get its benefit in the Hereafter if he dies with the faith of Islam. If he was not a Muslim, or became an apostate before death, all the good deeds he had done will be of no benefit to him.

The same rule applies to children. A Muslim can benefit from them in the Hereafter in that his children supplicate for his forgiveness after his death; and if he tried to train them to be pious, whatever good they do will pass on to him as long as they act righteously; and it is also possible that his pious children obtain his pardon by intercession — Maʿārif notes that a few hadiths report such intercession and its acceptance, especially that of young children who died before reaching puberty. Likewise, children benefit from their parents on condition of faith: if they were Muslims whose righteous deeds could not attain the level of their parents', Allah may place them at the high position of their parents, as He says, "We shall join their offspring with them" (52:21).

So wherever the Qur'an or hadith says that family connection avails nothing in the Hereafter — "when the Trumpet is blown there are no ties of kinship between them" (23:101); "the Day a man shall flee from his brother, his mother, his father" (80:34); "nor will a son be standing for his father in any way" (31:33) — the reference, on this reading, is to the disbelievers. And it holds so far that even the wife and children of a messenger, if they are not believers, gain nothing from his prophethood, as with the son of Nuh, the wife of Lut, and the father of Ibrahim, peace be upon them.

## Living it

The du'a of ayat 83–85 is a complete order of priorities you can pray in your own words tonight: **knowledge first, then to be joined with the righteous, then a life whose traces keep pointing others to good after you are gone, then the Garden of Bliss.** Nothing in it asks for wealth or standing for their own sake.

From ayah 84 and the scholars' conditions: it is not hypocrisy to want your life to be a good example. It becomes disease the moment the aim shifts to setting yourself *above* people rather than drawing them to good, or to being credited with a virtue you do not possess, or when reaching it costs you obedience to Allah.

From ayat 86–87: Ibrahim's prayer for his father was made while there was still hope of guidance for him — that is the space in which such du'a lives. And carry, as Ibrahim did, a fear not of punishment alone but of standing disgraced on that Day.

From ayat 88–89: everything the passage strips away — wealth, sons, the people you would have counted on — is exactly what a person spends a life accumulating as security. What Ibn Kathir says avails on that Day is faith in Allah, sincere devotion to Him, and turning away from shirk. And on the majority's reading, wealth and family do become useful again — but only *through* a sound heart, never instead of one. So the question the passage leaves is not "how much have I gathered" but "in what state will this heart come before Allah."

passages.title: Paradise brought near, the Fire displayed
passages.tafsir:
**These six ayat stop describing the Day of Judgement and begin staging it.** Two destinations are wheeled into view before the eyes of those who are headed for them — Paradise drawn near to those mindful of Allah, the Fire pulled out into the open before the astray — and then a question is put to the idol-worshippers that they cannot answer, followed by the collapse of everything they had trusted. What holds ayat 90–95 together is a single courtroom scene: the sight, the interrogation, the sentence.

Ibn Kathir titles this whole section "Those Who Have Taqwa and the Astray on the Day of Resurrection, and the Arguments and Sorrow of the Erring."

## Ayah 90: Paradise is brought to its people

**"And Paradise will be brought near to those mindful of Allah."**

Ibn Kathir explains أُزْلِفَتِ الْجَنَّةُ — *uzlifat al-jannah*, "brought near" — as meaning "it will be brought close to its people, adorned and decorated for them to behold it." Two things are happening at once. Paradise moves; and it is beautified for the viewing.

**Who are its people?** Ibn Kathir defines them not by a label but by a life: "the pious who preferred it to whatever was in this world, and strove for it in this world." That is a working definition of *taqwā* — mindfulness of Allah that actually costs something. They *preferred* Paradise: every time this world and the next asked for the same hour, the same money, the same loyalty, they chose the next. And they *strove*: preference alone was not the qualification; effort was. So when the Garden is brought near, it is being brought near to people who had already leaned towards it their whole lives.

## What they arrive carrying — the sound heart

The commentary reaches this scene by way of the two ayat just before it. Ayat 88–89 named the Day "when neither wealth will be of any use nor sons, except to one who will come to Allah with a sound heart" (*qalb salīm*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks that phrase, and it tells us what those mindful of Allah in ayah 90 brought with them.

**What "sound heart" means.** Literally it means a *healthy* heart. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that here it means the heart of a believer which testifies to the Oneness of Allah and is pure from shirk. The same interpretation is reported, in different wordings, from Mujāhid, Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab (may Allah have mercy on them). Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab put it starkly: the sound heart is only that of a believer, because the heart of a disbeliever is *sick*. Alongside this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the Qur'an's own words: "In their hearts there is a malady" (2:10).

So health of the heart is not measured in sentiment or sincerity-in-general. It is measured in Tawhid. A heart with shirk in it is, in the Qur'an's own vocabulary, a diseased organ.

**Two readings of "except".** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a genuine difference among the commentators over how the exception in ayah 89 works:

- *Some* commentators read it as what Arabic grammar calls a *munqaṭiʿ* (disconnected) exception — a type of exception that does not actually pull anything out of the preceding statement, but says instead that the thing denied in the first sentence is found in something else altogether. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a simple illustration: someone asks whether Zaid has wealth and children, and the reply comes, "No — his wealth and children are nothing but his sound heart." On this reading, wealth and sons help *nobody*, believer or disbeliever; what helps, in their place, is the sound heart, meaning true faith and righteous deeds.
- *The majority*, however, read it as an ordinary exception: wealth and children *may* be of benefit — but only to the one who comes to Allah with a sound heart, that is, with faith and righteous deeds. To a disbeliever they are of no use at all.
