A crowd of them gathered. They did not leave the miracle open-ended; they specified it. They demanded that Ṣāliḥ **immediately** bring forth **from the rock** — and they pointed to a certain rock standing there in their midst — **a she-camel that was ten months pregnant**.

Every element of that demand is designed to make failure certain. Not any rock: *that* rock, the one they were pointing at, so no substitution was possible. Not later: immediately, so no preparation was possible. Not any camel: one at a precise and advanced stage of pregnancy, so no ordinary animal could be passed off as the answer.

Ṣāliḥ, upon him be peace, then did something remarkable. Ibn Kathir says he **made them promise that if he responded to their request, they would believe in him and follow him** — and they agreed to that. He would not let the miracle be a spectacle. He bound it to a commitment first, so that afterwards no one could say they had merely been curious.

Then, Ibn Kathir tells us, the Prophet of Allah Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him, **stood and prayed**, and then he prayed to Allah to grant them their request. Pause on that. Facing a hostile crowd that had just called him bewitched, his response was not a debate. It was prayer, and then supplication.

And the rock to which they had pointed **split open, revealing a she-camel that was ten months pregnant, exactly as they had requested.**

Then comes the line that should stop every reader: **"So some of them believed, but most of them disbelieved."**

They had chosen the terms. They had watched the terms be met to the letter. They had given their word. And most of them still walked away. This is the passage's quiet argument about human nature: the problem was never insufficient evidence. A heart that has already decided will not be moved by a rock splitting open in front of it. Ayah 158 will say the same thing in Allah's own words — *most of them are not believers*.

## "It has a right to drink, and you have a right to drink" (155)

The camel does not merely appear; she comes with a rule attached: *Here is a she-camel: it has a right to drink, and you have a right to drink, each on a day, known.*

Ibn Kathir explains the arrangement simply: **"she will drink from your water one day, and on the next day you will drink from it."** Alternate days. Nothing complicated, nothing burdensome — and nothing ambiguous either, which is why the ayah calls it *a day, known*. The trial had clear terms, so that no one could later plead confusion.

And it was not a one-sided imposition. Ibn Kathir describes what the arrangement actually looked like in practice: **the she-camel stayed among them for a while, drinking the water, eating leaves and grazing, and they benefitted from her milk, which they took in sufficient quantities for every one to drink his fill.**

Sit with that. The sign was not a burden dropped on their town; it was a provision. Their "sacrifice" was to wait their turn at the water, and in exchange they were fed. And this went on, Ibn Kathir says, **for a long time**.

## "And touch her not with harm" (156)

*And touch her not with harm, lest the torment of a Great Day should seize you.*

The wording is deliberately wide. Not "do not kill her" — **do not *touch* her with harm**. The smallest hostile hand laid on her is forbidden. When Allah wants a boundary respected, He often draws the line well before the cliff edge, because the person who plays at the edge of a prohibition is already halfway over it.

Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and exact: **he warned them of the punishment of Allah if they should do her any harm.** So they were not ambushed. The rule was known, the consequence was named, and the naming came before the deed.

## "But they killed her, and then they became regretful" (157)

Ibn Kathir marks the timing precisely: the camel had been among them a long while, and **after this had gone on for a long time, and the time for their destruction drew near, they conspired to kill her.** The killing was not a sudden flare of temper. Ibn Kathir's word is *conspired*: it was agreed upon before it was carried out.

Then the ayah adds words that are among the most sobering in the story: **"and then they became regretful."**

Regret arrived. It simply arrived too late. In the very next breath the Qur'an says, *So, the torment overtook them.* The regret and the ruin sit almost side by side.

This is worth naming honestly, because it is the practical lesson of the passage. Regret has a season. Felt while the door is still open, it is the most valuable thing a person owns. Felt after the punishment has been set in motion, it changes nothing at all. Thamūd were not people who never felt sorry. They were people who felt sorry at the wrong time.

## "So, the torment overtook them" (158)

Ibn Kathir describes what came:

> **Their land was shaken by a strong earthquake, and there came to them an overwhelming Sayhah (shout) which took their hearts from their places. They were overtaken by events which they were not expecting, so they were left (dead), lying prostrate in their homes.**

Ibn Kathir's phrase "took their hearts from their places" conveys a terror that seized them from the inside while the ground moved beneath them. And note his last two touches. They were overtaken by **events which they were not expecting** — the very people who had been warned in the plainest terms in ayah 156 were, in the event, taken by surprise. That is what heedlessness does: it converts a clear warning into a shock.

And they were left **in their homes** — in the one place a person expects to be safe. Whatever shelter they had built for themselves was no shelter at all against the command of Allah.

## "Verily, in this is indeed a sign, yet most of them are not believers"

Now the demand of ayah 154 comes full circle. They asked for an *āyah*, a sign. They received it, and destroyed it, and were destroyed. And Allah says: **in this is indeed a sign**. The camel was a sign for Thamūd; the ruin of Thamūd is a sign for everyone after them. Nothing is wasted; even the wreckage teaches.

And then, immediately: **"yet most of them are not believers."** The same verdict Ibn Kathir gave when the rock split open: some believed, most disbelieved. Signs do not compel faith. They establish the truth and leave the heart free — which is precisely why the heart is answerable.

## "And verily, your Lord He is indeed the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful" (159)

The passage ends on two of Allah's names held together: **al-ʿAzīz**, the All-Mighty, and **al-Raḥīm**, the Most Merciful.

Each of them illuminates something in the story just told. **The All-Mighty**: He split the rock at a Prophet's supplication, and He shook a proud people into stillness with an earthquake and an overwhelming shout. Their numbers, their standing, the plan agreed among them — none of it counted for anything against Him.

**The Most Merciful**: and where was mercy in this account? Everywhere before the end. Mercy sent them a Prophet who called them to worship their Lord. Mercy answered the challenge they set, on the exact terms they set. Mercy gave the sign a form that fed them — milk enough for every one of them to drink his fill — rather than merely astonishing them. Mercy named the consequence before they acted. And mercy waited, through the whole long period the camel lived among them.

For the Prophet ﷺ hearing this — for it is *your Lord* that the ayah names — and for every believer since, the pairing is comfort and caution in one breath: the Mighty One is Merciful, so do not despair; and the Merciful One is Mighty, so do not presume.

## Living it

**The problem is rarely the evidence.** Thamūd chose the terms of the miracle, watched them met exactly, and most of them still disbelieved. When someone will not accept the truth, the missing ingredient is usually not proof. Ask that of yourself before you ask it of anyone else.

**Take your turn.** The test of ayah 155 was almost absurdly small: alternate days at the water, and be fed in return. Much of what ruins people is not a grand temptation but a small share they refuse to give up — a turn, a right, a portion that belongs to someone else.

**Do not stand at the edge of a line.** Ayah 156 forbids even *touching* her with harm. Boundaries are drawn with margin for a reason.

**Regret now, while it counts.** Ayah 157 shows that a person can feel every bit of the remorse and still be too late. The distance between Thamūd and safety was not a feeling; it was timing.

passages.title: Lot confronts his people and prays for rescue
passages.tafsir:
These ten ayat carry the story of Lot (Lūṭ, peace be upon him) from the opening verdict on his people to the moment he stops arguing with them and turns to Allah instead. What holds the passage together is a single arc: a prophet's call is offered (160–164), the specific sin is named and challenged (165–166), the people answer not with argument but with a threat of exile (167), and Lot responds by disowning the deed outright (168) and praying to be rescued from it (169). The passage is a study in what a believer does when speech has run out.

## Who Lot was, and where this happened

Ibn Kathir opens by placing the man. He was Lūṭ ibn Hārān ibn Āzar, the nephew of Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl, peace be upon them both, and Allah sent him to a mighty nation during Ibrāhīm's own lifetime. His people lived in Sadūm (Sodom) and the settlements around it — a place Ibn Kathir says Allah destroyed and turned into a putrid, stinking lake, well known in the land of al-Ghūr (the Jordan Valley), bordering the mountains of Jerusalem, between those mountains and the land of al-Karak and ash-Shawbak.

That geographical detail is not decoration. Ibn Kathir is pointing at a place on the map — somewhere a traveller could still stand beside.

Note what ayah 161 calls him: **"their brother Lot."** By the lineage Ibn Kathir gives, he was not descended from them at all; he came from Ibrāhīm's household. Yet the ayah names him their brother. Read alongside Ibn Kathir's account, the brotherhood is that of a man living among them and speaking to them as one of their own, not as an outsider throwing stones from a distance. A warner who despises the people he warns has already failed.

## The call: four sentences, nothing new

Ibn Kathir summarises Lot's mission in a line: he called them to Allah, to worship Him alone with no partner or associate, and to obey the Messenger whom Allah had sent to them; and he forbade them from disobeying Allah and from the sin they had invented — a sin, Ibn Kathir says, that was unknown on earth before their time.

Ayah 160 states the verdict before a word of the exchange is reported: **"The people of Lot rejected the messengers."** Then come the four ayat that carry his call (161–164):

- **"Will you not fear Allah?"** (161) — an appeal to *taqwā*, the mindfulness of Allah that makes a person watch what they do because they know Allah is watching. Ibn Kathir keeps the Arabic word here: *will you not have Taqwa?*
- **"Verily, I am a trustworthy Messenger to you"** (162) — the Arabic is *amīn*, trustworthy. He is not claiming brilliance or authority; he is claiming that nothing he delivers has been tampered with.
- **"So, have Taqwa of Allah, and obey me"** (163) — obedience to the messenger is folded into fear of Allah, because the messenger brings nothing of his own.
- **"No reward do I ask of you for it; my reward is only from the Lord of all that exists"** (164) — the call costs them nothing, and his wage is not in their hands at all.

## Naming the sin (165–166)

Ayah 165 is a question, not a sermon — Ibn Kathir renders it: **"Go you in unto the males of Al-ʿĀlamīn (people)"** — and ayah 166 completes it: **"And leave those whom Allah has created for you to be your wives? Nay, you are a trespassing people!"**

Ibn Kathir's summary of these two ayat is careful and worth repeating exactly as he puts it: the Prophet of Allah forbade them from committing evil deeds and from intercourse with males, *and he taught them that they should have intercourse with their wives whom Allah had created for them*. The prohibition came with its lawful alternative attached. Lot did not merely condemn; he redirected.

Two things in the wording carry the argument.

**"What your Lord has created for you."** That is how Maʿārif ul Qurʾān renders the opening of ayah 166. The ayah does not simply say "your wives" and leave it there — it says what your *Lord* created *for you*. The charge is not that they broke a social custom but that they walked past a provision their own Lord had made.

**"Nay, you are a trespassing people."** That is Ibn Kathir's rendering of the verdict: those who cross a boundary. The image is of a line drawn and deliberately stepped over.

### Two readings of one small word in ayah 166

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān stops on the word *min* in the phrase *min azwājikum*, "of your wives," and sets out two possibilities for what it is doing.

**First possibility:** the *min* is descriptive — translated above as "that is." The sense of the ayah is then: in order to satisfy your lust you go after men instead of your wives, whom Allah has given you to meet your natural urge. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān calls this, plainly, a proof of malignity — a desire that has turned against itself.

**Second possibility:** *min* means "from" or "out of," so that the ayah is pointing to a particular part of the body of your wives which was created for the satisfaction of that natural urge — and the unnatural act with them is totally unlawful. On this second interpretation, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān says, it has also been made clear that unnatural intercourse is not permitted with one's own wife.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds that in a hadith the Prophet ﷺ cast a curse on such a person. It reports this teaching citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, without naming the collection the hadith comes from — so we convey the teaching and do not attach it to a book we have not seen. The passage closes with *naʿūdhu billāhi minhu*, "we seek refuge with Allah from it."

What the two readings share is the passage's underlying logic: Allah created something for a purpose, and to depart from that purpose is to step over a line.

## Their answer: expulsion (167)

Ayah 167 records the reply, and it is not a reply. **"If you cease not, O Lot, verily, you will be one of those who are driven out!"** Ibn Kathir glosses "if you cease not" as *if you do not give up what you have brought* — the message itself — and "you will be one of those who are driven out" as *we will expel you from among us*.

They did not answer his question. They did not defend the act. They simply announced that the man who raised the subject would be removed from the town. Ibn Kathir links this to the parallel in Sūrat an-Naml, where the whole answer of his people was: **"Drive out the family of Lot from your city. Verily, these are men who want to be clean and pure!"** (27:56)

Sit with that. Purity itself became the accusation. A society can reach a point where the objection to a righteous man is not that he is wrong but that he is clean, and cleanliness is felt as an insult. Notice too that in that parallel the threat is aimed at his *family* as well as at him — which is exactly what his prayer in ayah 169 will take into account.

## Lot's disavowal (168)

**"I am indeed of those who disapprove with severe anger and fury your behaviour."**

The Arabic is *innī li-ʿamalikum mina l-qālīn*. Ibn Kathir renders *al-qālīn* as those who disapprove with severe anger and fury, and expands it in Lot's own voice: *of those who are outraged — I do not like it, I do not accept it, and I have nothing to do with you.* This is not mild disapproval kept politely to oneself. It is a public severing.

Ibn Kathir tells us precisely when Lot said it: **when he saw that they would not give up their ways and that they were persisting in their misguidance**, he declared his innocence of them. The declaration of innocence came *after* the argument had been exhausted, not instead of it. He questioned them, taught them the lawful alternative, and only when persistence was proven did he disown.

And note the object of the phrase: *li-ʿamalikum* — "of your **deed**." What he declares himself an enemy of is the act. The sentence is built around the thing done, not around a slur.

## The prayer (169)

**"My Lord! Save me and my family from what they do."**

They threatened him with expulsion; he asked Allah for rescue. Ibn Kathir places this immediately after the disavowal: *then he prayed to Allah against them* — the natural next move for a man who has no leverage left except his Lord.

Three things in the wording repay attention.

**"My Lord" — *Rabbi*.** Not a distant title. The same word ayah 166 used of the people who walked past their Lord's provision, now used by the one man clinging to Him.

**"Save me *and my family*."** He does not pray only for himself. The threat had named his household (27:56), and so does his prayer.

**"From what they do" — *mimmā yaʿmalūn*.** Not "from *them*." He asks to be delivered from what they *do* — and the translation before us fills in the sense as "from ˹the consequences of˺ what they do." It is the same root, *ʿamal*, that he used in ayah 168 when he said he detested their *deed*. What he hated is exactly what he asked to be saved from.

The passage leaves us there — at the point where a man who has said everything he can say turns and speaks to Allah instead.

## Living it

**Say the lawful thing, not only the forbidden one.** Ibn Kathir's summary of ayah 166 has Lot both forbidding and *teaching* — he pointed them to what Allah had created for them. Prohibition on its own leaves a person with nowhere to go.

**Expect the accusation to be your cleanliness.** The reply Lot received was not a rebuttal but an eviction notice, and the reason given in the parallel ayah was that his household wanted to be clean and pure (27:56). When that is the charge against you, you are in good company.

**Hate the deed, and say so about the deed.** Lot's fury in ayah 168 is attached to *ʿamal* — an action. That is the shape the Qur'an gives to a believer's anger here.

**Know when arguing ends and supplication begins.** Ibn Kathir marks the turn exactly: Lot declared his innocence and prayed *when he saw that they would not give up their ways*. He did not give up early, and he did not keep arguing forever. Between those two failures lies ayah 169 — the *duʿāʾ*, the personal calling upon Allah, that he made when speech had run out.

**Pray for your household, not just yourself.** Lot's rescue request had his family inside it from the first breath: *"Save me and my family."* The people we love belong in our supplications by name, not as an afterthought.

passages.title: Lot's family saved, the rain of destruction
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These six ayat are the closing movement of the story of Lūt (Lot), peace be upon him: he and his household are carried out to safety, one person is deliberately left behind, the rest are destroyed, and the passage ends by naming two of Allah's attributes. What holds it together is a single hinge — the word *najjā*, "to rescue." Ibn Kathir sets ayah 170 directly against the prayer that preceded it: Lūt "prayed to Allah against them and said: *My Lord! Save me and my family from what they do.*" Allah answers with the very same verb: "So, We saved him and his family, all." Everything after that — the exception in 171, the destruction in 172, the rain in 173 — is the shape that rescue took.

## Ayah 170: the prayer answered in its own words

*Fa-najjaynāhu wa-ahlahū ajmaʿīn* — "So, We saved him and his family, all" (Ibn Kathir's rendering).

The connective *fa-* ("so") places the answer immediately after the request. Lūt had asked, *Rabbi najjinī wa-ahlī* — "My Lord! Save me and my family." Allah replies with the same root and the same scope, and then adds a word the request did not contain: *ajmaʿīn*, "all." The answer comes back larger than what was asked for.

Look also at *what* he asked to be saved from: not from a punishment but *mimmā yaʿmalūn*, "from what they do." The deliverance he sought was deliverance out of that environment and its deeds.

Ibn Kathir fills in how the rescue physically happened, drawing on the parallel tellings of this story: "This is similar to what Allah says about them in Surat Al-Aʿraf and Surah Hud, and in Surat Al-Hijr, where Allah commanded him to take his family at night, except for his wife, and not to turn around when they heard the *Sayhah* as it came upon his people." Then comes the sentence that is the human centre of the whole passage: "So they patiently obeyed the command of Allah and persevered."

The rescue was real, but it still had to be walked out — at night, under instruction, with a hard condition attached: do not turn around. Obedience and patience were the form the deliverance took.

## Ayah 171: the one who stayed

*Illā ʿajūzan fi'l-ghābirīn* — "except an old woman, who was one of the doomed," or as Ibn Kathir renders it, "Except an old woman among those who remained behind." He identifies her plainly: "This was his wife, who was a bad old woman. She stayed behind and was destroyed with whoever else was left."

Two things are worth slowing down for.

**First, the exception is placed immediately after the word "all."** Ayah 170 says *ajmaʿīn* — every last one of his family; ayah 171 immediately carves out one person. The passage could have said simply "We saved his household." Instead it says *all*, then *except*, so that the exception reads as a decision rather than an oversight. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states why she was excluded: she "was an infidel and was agreeable to the unnatural act of the people of Lūt." She was not left behind for a lapse of manners but for where she herself stood. Being the wife of a prophet, sharing his house and his name, transferred no faith to her.

**Second, why "old woman"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question honestly. If she was in fact old, the word needs no explanation. But if she was not old, then "perhaps she was called 'old woman' for the reason that the prophet's wife is regarded like the mother of the Ummah, and to call a woman having many children as old is not unlikely." Either way, she is left in the text without a name — only a category: *fi'l-ghābirīn*, among those who remained behind.

## Ayah 172: "Then We utterly destroyed the rest"

*Thumma dammarnā'l-ākharīn* — "Then afterward We destroyed the others."

The word *thumma* ("then, afterward") puts the order of events into the grammar: rescue first, destruction second. The household is out before the sentence falls. And *al-ākharīn* — "the others" — is a name defined entirely by contrast with the household that was saved. In this passage humanity is sorted into just two groups: those Allah delivered, and the others.

## Ayah 173: a rain that was no mercy

*Wa-amṭarnā ʿalayhim maṭaran, fa-sāʾa maṭaru'l-mundharīn* — "And We rained on them a rain, and how evil was the rain of those who had been warned" (Ibn Kathir); Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it, "and subjected them to a terrible rain. So evil was the rain of those who were warned."

Ibn Kathir tells us what actually fell: "Allah sent upon the people a punishment which struck them all, and rained upon them stones of baked clay, piled up."

Notice the last word of the ayah: *al-mundharīn*, "those who had been warned." They are not called here the sinners or the transgressors but the warned ones. The warning had already reached them — Ibn Kathir describes Lūt as the one who "forbade them from committing evil deeds and intercourse with males, and he taught them that they should have intercourse with their wives whom Allah had created for them," and records that their whole response was to threaten him with expulsion. The rain fell on people who had been told.

**What jurists drew from this.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes a legal inference from the *manner* of the destruction: "if a man commits sodomy, he may be punished with throwing a wall on him or by throwing him down from a high place, as suggested by Hanafi scholars, because the people of Lūt (peace be upon him) were destroyed in a similar manner. Their township was lifted and thrown on the ground" (Shami, *Kitāb al-Ḥudūd*). This is reported here as the reasoning of the Hanafi jurists, who derive the form of the penalty from the form of the divine punishment.

## Ayah 174: a sign, and still they do not believe

*Inna fī dhālika la-āyah, wa-mā kāna aktharuhum muʾminīn* — "Verily, in this is indeed a sign, yet most of them are not believers."

The ayah makes two statements and lets them stand side by side. The story just told is an *āyah* — a sign, a piece of evidence set up for anyone willing to read it. And the second half is deliberately deflating: even with all of that, "most of them are not believers." The evidence is not the problem. What people do with evidence is.

## Ayah 175: al-ʿAzīz, ar-Raḥīm

*Wa-inna rabbaka la-huwa'l-ʿAzīzu'r-Raḥīm* — "And verily your Lord, He is indeed the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful."

The passage ends by naming two attributes it has just shown in action, and in that order. *Al-ʿAzīz*, the All-Mighty: the city was destroyed and nothing stood in the way. *Ar-Raḥīm*, the Most Merciful: Lūt and his household walked out of it alive. These are not two moods in Allah that take turns; they are two attributes of one Lord, affirmed as He has described Himself, without likening them to anything in creation and without emptying them of their meaning. The same night held both — the stones and the road out — and the ayah insists the reader see them as belonging to the same Lord.

The wording is also personal rather than abstract: not "the Lord" but *rabbuka*, "**your** Lord," spoken in the second person.

## Living it

- **Ask to be saved from the sin, not only from the consequence.** The prayer that ayah 170 answers is *save me and my family from what they do* — and it is a prayer made for a household, not only for oneself.
- **Rescue can require a long obedience.** Ibn Kathir's summary of the deliverance is not a magical removal but a command to travel by night, a condition not to turn around, and then: "So they patiently obeyed the command of Allah and persevered."
- **Closeness to righteous people saves no one on its own.** Ayah 171 is the whole argument: the wife of a prophet, inside the household named as saved, lost because of what she herself believed and approved.
- **The rescue comes before the ruin.** *Thumma* — "then afterward." The believers were clear before the sentence fell.

passages.title: Shuʿayb and the honest measure
passages.tafsir:
Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) is sent to a people the Qur'an names here not by tribe but by the object of their devotion — a tree. His mission comes down to two things joined at the root: fear the One who made you, and give people the full amount you owe them.

That pairing is what holds ayat 176–184 together. The first half (176–180) is the messenger's opening address: a call to taqwā, a claim to trustworthiness, a call to obedience, and a refusal of any fee. The second half (181–184) is what that call meant *for these people in particular*: honest scales, honest measures, honest dealing. The passage then closes in ayah 184 by tying the marketplace back to the Creator — which is where it began.

## "The companions of the Thicket" — who were they?

Ayah 176 does not name them as a tribe. It names them by what they revered: **aṣḥāb al-Aykah**, the people of the *Aykah*. Ibn Kathir explains that the Aykah was a tree they used to worship; it was also said to be a group of trees tangled together, like trees in a thicket.

Ibn Kathir holds that these were the people of Madyan, "according to the most correct view," and that Shuʿayb was one of them. He cites Isḥāq bin Bishr for the view that the companions of al-Aykah were Shuʿayb's own people, and reports that someone besides Juwaybir said plainly: the dwellers of al-Aykah and the people of Madyan are one and the same. Ibn Kathir adds the scholar's caution — *and Allah knows best.*

He notes that another opinion exists, that they were different nations with two identities. Some, he says, did not notice the point about the name, so they thought the dwellers of al-Aykah were different from the people of Madyan and claimed that Shuʿayb was sent to two nations; some said three. His own conclusion is that they were one nation described differently in different places — and the evidence he gives is the content of the preaching itself: **Shuʿayb preached to them and commanded them to be fair in their weights and measures, the same as is mentioned in the story of Madyan.** Same prophet, same sin named, same remedy.

**A small word that carries the whole point.** The expected phrasing, Ibn Kathir observes, would have been *when their brother Shuʿayb said to them* — and that is exactly what Allah did not say. Ayah 177 says simply, *when Shuʿayb said to them*. Ibn Kathir catches this. Shuʿayb was their brother by blood; he is not described as belonging to them here because of the meaning that was inherent in the name they had been given — a name denoting their deification of the Aykah. They had defined their identity by a tree they worshipped, and the wording keeps a prophet of Allah out of that description. It is one of those places where what the Qur'an *does not* say is the commentary.

## The messenger's opening (177–180)

Ayat 177–180 are the opening address, and reading them slowly is worth doing.

**"Will you not fear Allah?" (177).** The word behind "fear" here is *taqwā*, which Ibn Kathir keeps in Arabic rather than translating — he renders the ayah, "Will you not have Taqwa?" Watch where it sits: it comes *first*, before any mention of scales. The commercial fraud that follows is addressed only after this. And the same word returns twice more in the passage, as a command in ayah 179 and again at the close in ayah 184.

**"I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you" (178).** The Arabic word is *amīn* — trustworthy. Set it beside what he will demand three ayat later. He is asking a community that will be commanded to stop short-weighing to accept a man whose stated credential is precisely that he can be trusted. The claim and the command turn on the same quality: one worn by the messenger, one asked of the people.

**"So fear Allah, and obey me" (179).** Taqwā is repeated, now as a command rather than a question, and the ayah joins it directly to obeying the messenger. The two are not offered as separate items; the ayah puts them in one breath.

**"I do not ask you for any reward for this; my reward is only from the Lord of all worlds" (180).** This sentence removes an excuse. He wants nothing from them. His account, as he states it, is with the Lord of all worlds, not with them.

## The command: give full measure

Ayah 181: **"Give full measure, and cause no loss to others."**

Ibn Kathir writes that Allah commanded them to give full measure and forbade them to give short measure, and his paraphrase is as plain as the ayah: when you give to people, give them full measure, and do not cause them loss by giving short measure while taking full measure when you are the one receiving. He compresses it into a rule anyone can carry: **"Give as you take, and take as you give."**

That is the exact shape of the sin. It is not that they could not measure. It is that they had two standards — full when goods came in, short when goods went out. The ayah names such people *al-mukhsirīn*: those who cause loss. The trader thinks he is the one profiting; the Qur'an names him by the loss he inflicts.

**Ayah 182: "Weigh with an even balance."** Ibn Kathir notes simply that the balance here is the scales. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the word *qisṭās*: some scholars held it to be a Roman word meaning justice, while others took it as an Arabic word derived from *qisṭ*, which is also used for justice. Either way the sense is the same, and Maʿārif states it usefully — it means making use of the scale and other measuring tools in a straight and correct manner, **where there is no possibility of weighing less.** That is a higher bar than "do not cheat." It asks you to arrange your instruments and your habits so that weighing short is not even available to you.

**Ayah 183: "And do not defraud people of their property."** The verb is *tabkhasū*; Ibn Kathir glosses it in three words: do not shortchange them.

## The reach of ayah 183: not only in the marketplace

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the ayah in a way most readers will not expect, and it is the most practically searching point in the passage.

What ayah 183 means, it says, is that **it is unlawful to reduce any quantity or amount from that which has been contracted with anyone, whether it is a measurable thing or otherwise.** So — and this is stated explicitly — if a servant or a labourer does not work his full time at his workplace, he too is included in this warning.

The proof offered is a narration Imam Mālik (may Allah have mercy on him) reports in his *Muwaṭṭaʾ*: Sayyidunā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) noticed that someone did not join in the ʿAṣr prayer. He enquired about the reason, and the man offered some excuse. ʿUmar then said to him: **ṭaffafta** — "you have reduced in measuring."

Prayer is not something to be measured. That is precisely the force of ʿUmar's word, and Imam Mālik draws the conclusion out after quoting it: this command is not restricted to measurable things. Rather, **performing any obligation less than due is included in the prohibition highlighted in this verse** — and, Maʿārif adds, in Sūrah at-Taṭfīf.

Sit with that. The ayah lands on the shopkeeper's thumb on the scale, yes. But by the reasoning Maʿārif sets out, it reaches the employee paid for eight hours who gives six; the work handed in knowingly half-done; the duty owed and quietly delivered light — including obligations owed to Allah Himself.

## "Nor spread corruption in the land"

The second half of ayah 183 moves from private fraud to public havoc. Ibn Kathir explains *wa lā taʿthaw fi'l-arḍ mufsidīn* as engaging in banditry, and he adds that this is like the ayah: **"And sit not on every road, threatening"** (7:86).

So the two halves of one ayah sit side by side: shaving what is owed in a transaction, and taking by force on the road. Ibn Kathir's gloss puts them under a single prohibition. Cheating and violence turn out to be two settings of one appetite — taking from people what is not yours, quietly if you can, forcibly if you must.

## Ayah 184: the argument comes back to the Creator

**"And fear the One who created you and all the earlier peoples."**

Ibn Kathir says that Shuʿayb is here making them fear the punishment of Allah — the One who created them and created their forefathers. He notes that this is like what Mūsā (peace be upon him) said: *"Your Lord and the Lord of your ancient fathers"* (26:26).

On *al-jibillata al-awwalīn*, "the generations of the men of old," Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, as-Suddī, Sufyān bin ʿUyaynah and ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam said it means that He created the early generations. And Ibn Zayd recited: *"And indeed he — Shayṭān — did lead astray a great multitude of you"* (36:62).

Why end an argument about scales by naming Allah as the Creator of everyone who ever lived? Because of what Ibn Kathir says is happening in the ayah: Shuʿayb is putting the fear of Allah's punishment before them, and he identifies Allah by an act no customer can match — the creating of them and of every generation before them. Short-weighing depends on nobody noticing. This ayah does not argue about the scales at all; it changes who is in the room.

## Living it

The passage asks something narrower and harder than "be a good person":

- **Audit your instruments, not only your intentions.** Maʿārif's phrase is the standard: measure in such a way that weighing less is not even possible.
- **Apply one rule in both directions.** Ibn Kathir's line is worth memorising — *give as you take, and take as you give.* Whatever fullness you expect when it is coming to you, hand over when it is going out.
- **Extend it past goods.** Maʿārif applies it to anything contracted, measurable or not — a labourer's hours included — and ʿUmar's rebuke carries it as far as a missed prayer. Anything given short of its due is short measure.
- **Keep the order of the ayat.** Taqwā first (177, 179), honest dealing second (181–183), taqwā again at the close (184). Ethics here is not a policy bolted onto belief; the passage grows it out of belief and seals it with belief.

Notice, finally, what the passage records of Shuʿayb himself. He asks for no reward at all (180), and he ends not with an appeal to their profit but with a reminder of the One who created them and everyone before them (184). That is the shape of sincere calling to Allah — no price on it, and no discount on the truth.

passages.title: The Day of the Shadow overtakes the Forest
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat close the story of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) and his people: their scornful reply to him, the reckless challenge they threw at the sky, his calm answer, and the punishment that came in exactly the shape they had asked for. What holds the passage together is that terrible symmetry — a people demand a piece of heaven, and heaven obliges.

## The reply of a people who had already decided (185–186)

Ibn Kathir introduces their answer with an observation worth pausing over. Allah tells us how Shu'ayb's people responded, "and how it was like the response of Thamud to their Messenger – for they were of like mind." Different nations, different centuries, and a resemblance in how they met the truth when it arrived uninvited. Ibn Kathir traces that resemblance to something in the people themselves: they were of like mind.

Their answer in ayah 185 is **إِنَّمَآ أَنتَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُسَحَّرِينَ** — "You are only one of those bewitched." Ibn Kathir glosses it plainly: "you are one of those who are affected by witchcraft." Notice what the accusation does. It does not engage a single thing he said. It reclassifies the speaker. If the man is under a spell, his words need no reply — they are symptoms, not arguments. And the particle **إِنَّمَا** ("you are *only*") is the sound of a case being closed before it is opened.

Ayah 186 adds two more layers. First, **وَمَآ أَنتَ إِلَّا بَشَرٞ مِّثۡلُنَا** — "you are only a human being like us." A messenger who eats, sleeps and walks among them cannot, in their reckoning, be carrying anything from the heavens. Then, **وَإِن نَّظُنُّكَ لَمِنَ ٱلۡكَٰذِبِينَ**. Ibn Kathir reads this as: "we think you are deliberately lying to us in what you say, and Allah has not sent you to us."

Read the two ayat together and the accusations quietly contradict each other. A bewitched man is a victim — confused, not culpable. A liar is fully in command of himself and choosing deception. They level both charges in the same breath, which tells you these are not conclusions arrived at by weighing evidence. They are whatever came to hand. Rejection first; reasons afterwards.

## "Then drop the sky on us" (187)

**فَأَسۡقِطۡ عَلَيۡنَا كِسَفٗا مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ إِن كُنتَ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ** — "So cause pieces of the sky to fall upon us, if you are of the truthful."

Ibn Kathir sets three explanations of **كِسَفًا** side by side from the early authorities, without ruling between them:

- **Ad-Dahhak**: "One side of the heavens."
- **Qatadah**: "A piece of the heaven."
- **As-Suddi**: "A punishment from heaven."

Whether they were picturing a fragment or half the sky, the demand is the same in spirit — and Ibn Kathir places it alongside similar demands the Qur'an records elsewhere. He notes that this "is like what the Quraysh said": that they would not believe until a spring was made to gush forth from the earth for them (17:90), and among their conditions, "Or you cause the heaven to fall upon us in pieces, as you have pretended, or you bring Allah and the angels before us face to face" (17:92) — the same word *kisafan*, the same theatre. He also cites the chilling words recorded in 8:32: "O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones on us from the sky." Ibn Kathir's comment on Shu'ayb's people is that they spoke "in a stubborn and obstinate manner" — this was not a request for evidence but a dare.

There is a hard lesson buried in the comparison. People who ask for a catastrophe as proof are betting that nothing will happen. They are treating the sky as decoration. The Qur'an shows us the moment the bet is called.

## Shu'ayb's answer (188)

**قَالَ رَبِّيٓ أَعۡلَمُ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ** — "My Lord knows best whatever you do."

One short sentence, and he does not take the bait. He does not attempt to summon the punishment they ordered; that was never his to command. Ibn Kathir unfolds the meaning: "Allah knows best about you, and if you deserve that, He will punish you therewith, and He will not treat you unjustly."

Two things are affirmed at once. Allah's knowledge is complete and exact — He knows *what you do*, the deeds themselves, not merely the noise they are making at this moment. And His justice is perfect: whatever comes will be earned, never more than earned. Shu'ayb hands the matter over to the One who owns it and steps out of the way. For anyone who has ever been mocked for their faith and felt the urge to make something happen to prove a point, this ayah is the model: state the truth, entrust the outcome, do not negotiate with a dare.

## The Day of the Shadow (189)

**فَكَذَّبُوهُ فَأَخَذَهُمۡ عَذَابُ يَوۡمِ ٱلظُّلَّةِ** — "So they rejected him, and were seized by the torment of the Day of the Shadow."

Ibn Kathir's comment is the hinge of the whole passage: "This is what they asked for, when they asked for a part of the heaven to fall upon them." He then describes what came. Allah made their punishment "in the form of intense heat which overwhelmed them for seven days, and nothing could protect them from it." Then He sent a cloud to shade them, and they ran towards it seeking its shade from the heat. When all of them had gathered underneath it, "Allah sent sparks of fire and flames and intense heat upon them, and caused the earth to convulse beneath them, and He sent against them a mighty **Sayhah** which destroyed their souls." (*Sayhah* is the Arabic word Ibn Kathir uses here; elsewhere in his comment on this passage he refers to the same thing as the Blast that came upon other nations.)

Ibn Kathir supports this with a narration that Muhammad bin Jarir reported from Yazid al-Bahili, who said: "I asked Ibn 'Abbas about this ayah." Ibn 'Abbas answered that Allah sent upon them thunder and intense heat, and it terrified them — they entered their houses and it pursued them to the innermost parts of their houses and terrified them further, so they ran fleeing from their houses into the fields. "Then Allah sent upon them clouds which shaded them from the sun, and they found it cool and pleasant, so they called out to one another until they had all gathered beneath the cloud, then Allah sent fire upon them." Ibn 'Abbas concluded: "That was the torment of the Day of Shadow, indeed that was the torment of a Great Day."

The detail that they *called out to one another* is the most haunting line in the account. The relief felt so genuine that they invited each other into it. Nobody was dragged. They gathered themselves, gratefully, under their own destruction.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same event, citing **Ruh al-Maʿani**: Allah sent down such extreme heat that they could find comfort neither inside their houses nor outside; then He sent down a mass of dark cloud over a nearby forest, under which there was a cool breeze; and as the entire people were distressed by the excessive heat, they ran to take shelter under it. "When all of them assembled under the cover of the cloud, it rained fire instead of water. Thus the whole nation was burnt to ashes."

Sit with the shape of it. They had asked for something to fall on them *from* the sky. What fell was not a rock hurled at them from a distance — it was the very thing they had run toward for mercy. Their shelter was their punishment. Ibn Kathir calls it "an exact recompense": they got precisely what they ordered, delivered in the one form they would never have suspected. As he puts it, "it was fitting that something they never thought would happen should befall them."

## Why *this* punishment, and not another

Here Ibn Kathir opens up something that quietly answers a question many readers have: why is the destruction of Shu'ayb's people described differently in different surahs? His principle is that Allah "has mentioned how they were destroyed in three places in the Qur'an, in each of which it is described in a manner which fits the context." Each place names the aspect of the punishment that matches what has just been recounted:

- **In Surat al-A'raf** — the earthquake seized them, "and they lay (dead), prostrate in their homes." Why the earthquake? Because there they had said, "We shall certainly drive you out, O Shu'ayb, and those who have believed with you from our town, or else you all shall return to our religion" (7:88). Ibn Kathir explains: "They had sought to scare the Prophet of Allah and those who followed him, so they were seized by the earthquake." They threatened to shake the believers out of their homes; the ground shook them out of theirs.
- **In Surah Hud** — "And as-Sayhah seized the wrongdoers" (11:94). Why the Blast? Because there they had jeered, "Does your Salah command that we give up what our fathers used to worship, or that we give up doing what we like with our property? Verily, you are the forbearer, right-minded!" (11:87) — said, Ibn Kathir notes, "in a mocking, sarcastic tone." So "it was befitting that the Sayhah should come and silence them." They used their voices to sneer; a Voice from above ended the conversation.
- **And here** — they demanded a piece of the sky "in a stubborn and obstinate manner," so what befell them came from the sky, in the form they never expected.

This is worth carrying into the rest of your reading of the Qur'an. Where different places seem to give different accounts, Ibn Kathir's approach is to look for the wisdom in the selection: each retelling describes the event "in a manner which fits the context." Nothing is contradicted; something is chosen.

## The refrain returns (190–191)

**إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَةٗۖ وَمَا كَانَ أَكۡثَرُهُم مُّؤۡمِنِينَ** — "Surely in this is a sign. Yet most of them would not believe."

They had asked for a sign from the sky as their price for belief. There was indeed a sign in what happened — and ayah 190 tells us that even so, most would not believe. The demand of ayah 187 was never really about evidence. A sign does not manufacture faith in a heart that has already refused.

Then, immediately, ayah 191: **وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ** — "And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, the Most Merciful." Ibn Kathir's gloss on this pairing is short and exact: "He is All-Mighty in His punishment of the disbelievers, and Most Merciful towards His believing servants."

These two names are affirmed as they truly belong to Allah, without likening His might or His mercy to anything in creation and without emptying them of meaning. And notice how they sit together. A story that has just ended in ashes closes on **ar-Raḥīm**. On Ibn Kathir's reading the two are not in tension: the same Lord is overwhelming in His punishment of those who denied, and merciful toward those who believed. Note too that the ayah does not say "the Lord" but **رَبَّكَ**, "*your* Lord." The address is personal.

## Living it

Take the passage as a whole and it leaves three things in your hands.

**Watch how you dismiss what you do not want to hear.** Their reply in 185–186 never touched Shu'ayb's argument. It reclassified him — bewitched, and in the same breath a deliberate liar. It is a very human move, and it is not confined to prophets and their nations. When we find ourselves explaining away a person rather than answering what they actually said, the pattern here is worth remembering.

**Take Shu'ayb's posture when you are mocked.** "My Lord knows best whatever you do." He did not try to produce the catastrophe they ordered, and he did not argue about it. He named the truth and left the outcome with Allah, who — as Ibn Kathir puts it — "knows best about you… and He will not treat you unjustly." That is a settled place to stand, and it is available to anyone.

**And do not read comfort as approval.** The cruellest detail in this account is that the cloud really was cool. They were not mistaken about the shade; they were mistaken about what was inside it. They found it "cool and pleasant, so they called out to one another until they had all gathered beneath the cloud." Ease is not by itself a verdict on how we are living. It is worth asking, every so often, who sent the shade we are standing under.

passages.title: How the Qur'ān came down, and who attested it
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat answer a single question: *is this revelation genuine?* The passage answers it first by tracing the Qur'an's chain of custody (192–195), then by producing outside testimony (196–197), and finally by exposing that the objectors were never really asking about evidence at all (198–199).

## The chain of custody (192–195)

**"And truly, this is a revelation from the Lord of all the worlds" (192).** Ibn Kathir opens by saying that here Allah tells us about the Book which He revealed to His servant and Messenger Muhammad ﷺ. The pronoun *innahu* — "truly it" — refers to the Qur'an, which, Ibn Kathir notes, was described at the beginning of the sūrah as "a Reminder as a recent revelation from the Most Gracious" (26:5). The passage points back to what the sūrah said at its opening. And the phrase *latanzīlu Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn*, he explains, means simply: Allah has sent it down to you and revealed it to you.

The name used for the Sender is *Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn* — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "the Lord of all that exists." The Book comes down from the Lord of everything there is.

**"…which the trustworthy Spirit brought down" (193).** *Al-Rūḥ al-Amīn.* Ibn Kathir states that this is Jibrīl, peace be upon him, and lists the early authorities from the Salaf who said so: Ibn ʿAbbās, Muḥammad bin Kaʿb, Qatādah, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, as-Suddī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, az-Zuhrī and Ibn Jurayj. He then adds a remark he does not make lightly: **"This is an issue concerning which there is no dispute."**

Az-Zuhrī pointed out that this ayah is like Allah's words, "Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl — for indeed he has brought it down to your heart by Allah's permission, confirming what came before it…" (2:97). The same angel, the same heart, the same descent.

**"…upon your heart" (194).** The Arabic is *ʿalā qalbik* — not "to your ears", not "into your hands", but onto the heart. Ibn Kathir glosses it: *"O Muhammad, free from any contamination, with nothing added or taken away."*

Set that gloss beside the description Allah gives the carrier in the previous ayah — *the trustworthy Spirit* — and the passage's own emphasis becomes plain: the one who brought it is called trustworthy, and what landed had nothing added to it and nothing taken from it. Between the Speech of Allah and the recitation heard by its first Arabic-speaking audience there was no editorial hand, no summarising, no forgetting.

**"…that you may be one of the warners."** Ibn Kathir explains the purpose clause: so that you may warn people with it of the punishment of Allah for those who go against it and disbelieve in it — *and* so that you may give glad tidings with it to the believers who follow it. That second half matters. The ayah says "warner", but the tafsir will not let us read warning as the whole job; the same Book that threatens the rejecter carries good news to the one who accepts.

**"…in a clear Arabic tongue" (195).** Ibn Kathir: *"this Qur'an which We have revealed to you, We have revealed in perfect and eloquent Arabic, so that it may be quite clear, leaving no room for excuses and establishing clear proof, showing the straight path."* Three things are packed in there. The Arabic is *perfect and eloquent* — a claim about the beauty of the text. It is *clear* — a claim about the accessibility of the meaning. And clarity has a consequence: in Ibn Kathir's own words, it leaves no room for excuses and establishes clear proof.

So the four ayat give a complete chain: **from Allah, by Jibrīl, onto the Prophet's ﷺ heart, in clear Arabic.** Source, carrier, receiver, medium. Every link is named and every link is certified.

## What "in a clear Arabic tongue" settles

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a conclusion from ayah 195 that shapes how Muslims handle the Book to this day: the words *bilisānin ʿarabiyyin mubīn* make clear that **the Qur'an is only that which is in the Arabic language.** A translation of a passage — or of the whole Book — into any other tongue cannot itself be called Qur'an.

From this the commentary states three practical rulings:

- **Ṣalāh.** The whole Ummah is unanimous that reciting a translation of the Qur'an in Urdu, Persian, English or any other language does not discharge the obligation of recitation in prayer, except in a case of extreme necessity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the jurists reported to have relaxed this rule later changed their view.
- **Naming.** Calling a bare Urdu rendering "the Urdu Qur'an", or an English one "the English Qur'an", is not right and amounts to disrespect of the Holy Book.
- **Printing and trade.** Printing, calling or trading something in the name of "Qur'an" when it does not carry the Arabic text is not permitted. (The author of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that he treated this subject in detail in his treatise *Taḥdhīr al-Ikhwān ʿan Taghyīr Rasm al-Qurʼān*.)

None of this demeans translation. A translation is how a non-Arab reaches the meaning, and this passage's own logic — clarity, no excuses — pushes people toward understanding. The point is one of identity, not of worth: the translation carries the meaning, but the Qur'an is the Arabic revelation itself.

## "And it is indeed in the scriptures of the former people" (196)

**Ibn Kathir's reading.** This Qur'an was mentioned and referred to in the previous Scriptures that were left behind by their Prophets, who foretold it in ancient times and more recently. Allah took a covenant from them that they would follow it, and the last of them stood and addressed his people with the good news of Aḥmad: "And when ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, said: O Children of Israel! I am the Messenger of Allah unto you, confirming the Tawrāh before me, and giving glad tidings of a Messenger to come after me, whose name shall be Aḥmad" (61:6).

**The word *zubur*.** Ibn Kathir explains that *zubur* here refers to Books. It is the plural of *az-Zabūr*, which is also the name used for the Book given to Dāwūd, peace be upon him. The same plural appears elsewhere with a different application: "And everything they have done is noted in *az-zubur*" (54:52) — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, that it is recorded against them in the books of the angels.

**A real difficulty, and its answer.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the tension honestly. Ayah 195 has just insisted that the Qur'an is the Arabic revelation. Ayah 196 then says "it" is in the scriptures of the former people — and it is well known that the Tawrāh, Injīl and Zabūr were not in Arabic. How can both be true?

The answer given, and attributed to the majority of the Ummah, is that **sometimes even the subject matter of the Qur'an is called "Qur'an" in a general sense**, because the real purpose of a book is the subjects it deals with. When ayah 196 says the Qur'an was in the earlier scriptures, it means those books included some Qur'anic subjects — not that the portions of the Tawrāh or Injīl that carried those subjects are themselves called Qur'an. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic that **no one in the Ummah** holds that view.

The commentary supports this with narrations. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Sayyidnā Maquil ibn Yasar (may Allah be pleased with him) a hadith in the *Mustadrak* of Ḥākim that the Prophet ﷺ said Sūrah al-Baqarah was given to him from *adh-dhikr al-awwal*, and Sūrah Ṭāhā, the Ṭawāsīn (all the sūrahs starting from Ṭā Sīn) and the Ḥawāmīm (all the sūrahs beginning with Ḥā) were given from the tablets of Sayyidnā Mūsā, peace be upon him, while Sūrah al-Fātiḥah was given to him from under the ʿArsh, the great Throne. Ṭabarānī, Ḥākim, Bayhaqī and others report on the authority of Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) that Sūrah al-Mulk is present in the Torah as well. And Sūrah al-Aʿlā says of its own teachings that these subjects also appeared in the earlier scriptures — the scriptures of Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm and Sayyidnā Mūsā, peace be upon them (87:18–19).

**Why the point is not merely technical.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the principle out: **the Qur'an is the name not only of its wordings but also of its meanings.** It gives a vivid illustration. If someone picked up Qur'anic words from different places and put them together to make a passage — *al-ḥamdu lillāhi'l-ʿAzīzi'r-Raḥīm alladhī lahu mulku's-samāwāt wa huwa Rabbu'l-ʿālamīn khāliqu kulli shayʼin wa huwa'l-mustaʿān* — it would not be called Qur'an, despite the fact that all those words are taken from the Qur'an. And likewise, only the meanings of the Qur'an, in whatever language they are rendered, cannot be regarded as Qur'an.

## The witness of the scholars of Banī Isrāʼīl (197)

Ayah 197 turns the earlier scriptures into an argument the objectors could actually check: *"Is it not a sign to them that the learned scholars of the Children of Israel knew it?"* Ibn Kathir paraphrases: is it not sufficient witness to the truth for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel found this Qur'an mentioned in the Scriptures which they study?

This is testimony from outside the family. Ibn Kathir says that **the fair-minded among them admitted** that the attributes of Muhammad ﷺ, his mission and his Ummah were mentioned in their Books — as was stated by those among them who believed, such as **ʿAbdullāh bin Salām and Salmān al-Fārisī**, and others who met the Prophet ﷺ. He also cites Allah's description of the awaited one: "Those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet who can neither read nor write…" (7:157) — which sharpens the question of where such a Book could have come from.

Note the restraint in the wording. Allah says the scholars *knew* it, and Ibn Kathir says the *fair-minded* among them admitted it. The ayah is not claiming that all of them accepted; it is saying the knowledge was there in their books, available to any honest reader.

## When evidence is not the real obstacle (198–199)

"And if We had revealed it unto any of the non-Arabs, and he had recited it unto them, they would not have believed in it."

Ibn Kathir titles this section **the intense disbelief of Quraysh**, and reads it as showing how stubbornly they resisted the Qur'an. Allah shows them the shape of their own hearts by imagining the opposite scenario: if this Book, with all its eloquence, had been revealed to a non-Arab who did not know one word of Arabic, and he had recited it to them, they still would not have believed in him. Whatever the packaging, the answer was already decided.

Ibn Kathir stacks parallel ayat alongside it:

- "And even if We opened to them a gate from the heaven and they were to keep on ascending thereto, they would surely say: *Our eyes have been dazzled*" (15:14–15).
- "And even if We had sent down unto them angels, and the dead had spoken unto them…" (6:111).
- "Truly, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe" (10:96).

Read the passage as a whole and its architecture is unmistakable. Ayat 192–195 establish the Qur'an's origin. Ayat 196–197 add corroboration from earlier revelation and its own scholars. Ayat 198–199 then say: and if you still refuse, understand that the failure is not in the evidence.

## Living it

*The reflections below are ways of taking the passage to heart, drawn from the meanings explained above.*

**Handle the chain with the reverence it deserves.** The Book you open was brought down by *al-Rūḥ al-Amīn*, the trustworthy Spirit, and set upon the Prophet's ﷺ heart — in Ibn Kathir's words, free from any contamination, with nothing added or taken away. That is what you are holding.

**Learn the Arabic you can, and honour what a translation is.** Translations are the door to the meaning, and ayah 195 makes clear that this message was revealed to be clear and to leave no room for excuses — but as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists, the Qur'an is the name of its wordings together with its meanings, so a translation serves the Qur'an rather than replacing it, and in ṣalāh it does not stand in for it.

**Take both halves of the message.** Ibn Kathir reminds us that "warner" in ayah 194 covers both sides: warning people of the punishment of Allah for those who go against the Book, and glad tidings for the believers who follow it. Both come from the same Book.

**Check your own objections.** Ayat 198–199 are a mirror before they are a rebuke. When someone finds a reason to keep the Qur'an at arm's length — the messenger, the language, the era, the community — the honest question is the one this passage puts to Quraysh: if that reason were removed, would you then believe? It is a warning against assembling a case for a verdict the heart has already reached.

passages.title: Denial that only ends at the punishment
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat trace the whole arc of a heart that refuses the truth: denial is placed inside them, they will not believe until the punishment is in front of their eyes, it arrives without warning, they beg for more time — and the passage closes by turning their own demand back on them. The unit is held together by a single chain of verbs, each hooked to the last, so that denial, punishment, panic and the plea for delay read as one unbroken movement.

## One sentence, not five

Notice the shape. Ayah 200 states what has happened to these hearts. Ayah 201 states the result — "they will not believe in it." Then ayah 202 begins with *fa-* ("so, then"): *fa-ya'tiyahum baghtatan*, "so it comes upon them suddenly." Ayah 203 again with *fa-*: *fa-yaqūlū*, "so they say." The grammar refuses to let the reader pause between stages. Refusal leads to the sudden arrival, the arrival leads to the plea, and the plea comes exactly one moment too late. Then ayah 204 breaks the chain with a question: *a-fa-bi-ʿadhābinā yastaʿjilūn* — "Do they really seek to hasten Our punishment?"

That last question is the hinge. It drags the whole scene out of the future and sets it against something the deniers were already saying to the Messenger ﷺ in the present.

## Ayah 200: what entered the hearts

*Kadhālika salaknāhu fī qulūb al-mujrimīn.* Ibn Kathir renders it, "Thus have We caused it to enter the hearts of the criminals," and the translation before us reads, "This is how We allow denial ˹to steep˺ into the hearts of…"

So what is the "it" that enters? Ibn Kathir answers the question directly rather than leaving the pronoun open: *thus We caused denial, disbelief, rejection and stubbornness to enter the hearts of the sinners.* The translation supplies the same word into the sentence. On this reading, what takes up residence inside these people is not a message they failed to grasp — it is the refusal itself. Whatever image we choose from the two renderings, entering or steeping, the point is the same: something was put into a place and stayed there. It is not that these men merely heard and shrugged.

Two things are worth holding together here. First, Allah is the one who says "We caused it to enter" — nothing in a human heart happens outside His will, and the Qur'an does not soften that. Second, He does not call them "the unfortunate" or "the misled" but *al-mujrimīn*, the criminals — people named for what they themselves have committed. The passage does not leave that tension hanging; the sūrah answers it a few ayat later, as we will see at the end.

## Ayah 201: faith that arrives too late

"They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment." Here Ibn Kathir glosses the pronoun differently, and deliberately: *(They will not believe in it), i.e., the truth.* Denial went in; the truth stays out. That is the whole tragedy in two pronouns.

Then he explains the terrible timing. They will believe only when *their excuses will be of no avail, and the curse will be upon them, and theirs will be an evil abode.*

This is the heart of the passage. Such people are not incapable of belief. They will believe — everyone believes, eventually. The problem is that belief has a deadline, and past that line it buys nothing. Faith is faith only while the unseen is still unseen; once the punishment is standing in front of you, assent is no longer a choice, it is a reflex.

## Fir'awn at the water's edge

Ibn Kathir gives this its human face, and he reaches for the figure this sūrah itself opened with. Mūsā had prayed against Fir'awn — "Our Lord! You have indeed bestowed on Fir'awn and his chiefs splendour and wealth in the life of this world" — and Allah answered, "Verily, the invocation of you both is accepted" (10:88–89). Ibn Kathir comments that this supplication took effect on Fir'awn: *he did not believe until he saw the painful torment.* Then, when the sea closed over him, "till when drowning overtook him, he said: I believe that none has the right to be worshipped but He in Whom the Children of Israel believe" — and the reply came, "and you were one of the mischief-makers" (10:90–91).

Fir'awn is ayah 201 in a single body: a man who spent a lifetime saying no, who found faith in the last second of it, and found it worth nothing. Ibn Kathir cites the same pattern more generally — "so when they saw Our punishment, they said: We believe in Allah Alone" (40:84).

## Ayat 202–203: it comes while they are not looking

*Baghtatan* — Ibn Kathir: *the punishment of Allah will come upon them suddenly.* And the Qur'an adds *wa-hum lā yashʿurūn*, rendered here as "while they perceive it not," or "when they least expect it." Not only do they not expect it; they have no inkling of it. A person can be entirely at ease and entirely out of time.

Hence the cry in ayah 203: *hal naḥnu munẓarūn* — "Can we be respited?", "Can we be allowed more time?"

Ibn Kathir's comment on this cry is quietly devastating. When they see the punishment, *they will wish they had a little more time so that they can obey Allah — or so they claim.* That last clause is not cynicism; Ibn Kathir points the reader to Allah's words to His Prophet ﷺ — "And warn mankind of the Day when the torment will come unto them" — running through to "that you would not leave" (14:44). The regret is real: Ibn Kathir says that *when every sinner and evildoer sees his punishment, he will feel intense regret.* But regret is not repentance, and a promise made under the blade is not a life.

## Ayah 204: the demand turned around

"Would they then wish for Our torment to be hastened on?" Ibn Kathir calls this *a denunciation and a threat* — and he tells us why it is aimed where it is. The deniers had been saying to the Messenger ﷺ, in his own words, *by way of denial, thinking it unlikely ever to happen*: "Bring Allah's torment upon us" (29:29). Allah describes the same behaviour elsewhere: "And they ask you to hasten on the torment" (29:53).

Read carefully, this is not bravado; it is disbelief speaking. They asked for the punishment precisely because they were sure it would never come. A man only dares the thing he has decided is impossible.

So the sequence is deliberately hard on their position. Ayah 203 has just recorded the words they will say on that Day — *give us more time* — and ayah 204 sets those words beside the words they are saying now — *bring it on, hurry it up*. It is the same mouth. The man begging for a delay at the end is the man who demanded speed at the beginning, and the only thing that changed in between is that he finally believed it was real.

## And Allah is never unjust

One glance just past our five ayat, because it answers the question ayah 200 raised. Ibn Kathir says that Allah then *tells us of His justice towards His creation, in that He does not destroy any nation until after He has left them with no excuse, by warning them, sending Messengers to them and establishing proof against them* — "And never did We destroy a township but it had its warners by way of reminder, and We have never been unjust," which he places alongside "And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger" (17:15).

So the passage that began with denial entering hearts is followed by *wa mā kunnā ẓālimīn* — "and We have never been unjust." No one is punished before being warned. Whatever these hearts became, they did not become it in the dark.

## Living it

**Do not schedule your repentance.** Ayah 203 is a recording of a request that will be refused. Every intention to fix things "later" is a small rehearsal of *hal naḥnu munẓarūn* — and the passage has already shown how that request is answered.

**Take the suddenness seriously.** *Baghtatan… wa-hum lā yashʿurūn.* The people in ayah 202 had no warning. Feeling fine is not evidence of being fine.

**Spend faith while it still costs something.** Fir'awn's confession was word-perfect and worth nothing, because it came after the water. Ibn Kathir's point is not that he said the wrong thing; it is that he said the right thing too late.

**Watch what you dismiss as improbable.** Ayah 204 exists because people treated the punishment as something that could never actually arrive, and turned that assumption into a challenge. Ibn Kathir names the motive plainly: denial, thinking it unlikely ever to happen. That posture is available to anyone who has quietly filed the promises of Allah under "not really."

passages.title: Years of enjoyment avail nothing at the end
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close the long warning of this sūrah with a single thought experiment. Suppose Allah lets the deniers go on enjoying life for years — and then what they were promised finally arrives. What will all those years have been worth? Ayah 207 answers the question the moment it is asked: nothing. And ayat 208–209 close off the last possible objection — no community was ever destroyed without warners, so no one can say they were wronged.

## The setting

Ibn Kathir treats ayat 200–209 as one continuous passage, and the ayat just before 205 set up its whole shape. The deniers, he says, will not believe in the truth "until they see the painful torment" — that is, until the point at which their excuses will be of no avail. And when they do see the punishment, they will ask, **"Can we be respited?"** — give us more time. Ibn Kathir's comment on that plea is quietly devastating: they will wish they had a little more time so that they can obey Allah — **"or so they claim."**

He points to Fir'awn as the proof. Mūsā prayed against him, and the invocation was answered (10:88–89); yet Fir'awn did not believe until he saw the painful torment — only when the drowning overtook him did he say that he believed in the One in Whom the Children of Israel believe, and the reply came that he had been one of the mischief-makers (10:90–91). Allah states the same pattern generally: when they saw Our punishment they said, "We believe in Allah alone" (40:84). Belief that waits until the punishment is visible arrives too late to count.

And their position is incoherent from both ends. Ibn Kathir calls ayah 204 — "Would they then wish for Our torment to be hastened on?" — a denunciation and a threat, because they used to say to the Messenger, out of denial and thinking it unlikely ever to happen, *"Bring Allah's torment upon us"* (29:29), and they used to ask him to hasten the torment (29:53). Today they mock the punishment as impossible; on the day it comes they will beg for the delay they are already being given.

That is the door into ayah 205.

## Ayah 205: "So tell me…"

أَفَرَءَيْتَ إِن مَّتَّعْنَٰهُمْ سِنِينَ — *"Imagine, O Prophet, if We allowed them enjoyment for years."*

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ personally. Translators render the opening as "So tell me", or "Think", or "Imagine" — and none of those is a request for information. It is an invitation to run the calculation and see where it lands, and, by extension, an invitation to every listener who is banking on more time.

Notice the verb. In ayah 205 Allah says **mattaʿnāhum**, "We gave them enjoyment"; in ayah 207 the same root returns as **yumattaʿūn**, "that with which they were being given enjoyment." Both are things done *to* them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point directly about the years in question: those given a long life in this world by Allah have received His grace upon them. The comfort of the deniers is not something they wrested from the world; it is a gift from the very One whose warning they are ignoring.

Ibn Kathir spells out that the premise covers both cases at once: *even if We delay the matter and give them respite for a short while or for a long time*, and then the punishment of Allah comes upon them — what good will their life of luxury do them then?

## Ayat 206–207: the arithmetic of the end

ثُمَّ جَآءَهُم مَّا كَانُوا۟ يُوعَدُونَ — "then there came to them what they had been threatened with."

Ibn Kathir renders the same phrase "that which they had been promised." Either way, the thing that arrives had been announced in advance. Nothing new appears on that day except the arrival itself — which is exactly why the warners of ayah 208 matter so much.

Then ayah 207: مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُم مَّا كَانُوا۟ يُمَتَّعُونَ — "would that enjoyment be of any benefit to them at all?" The verb is the one rendered *avail*: shall it be of any use to them. Ibn Kathir gathers three other places where the Qur'an applies the same measure:

- **79:46** — the Day they see it, it will be as if they had not tarried in this world except an afternoon or a morning. A whole life collapses into an evening.
- **2:96** — every one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years, *but the grant of such life will not save him even a little from punishment*. This is the direct answer to the plea for respite. More time is not a solution; it is only more of the same.
- **92:11** — "And what will his wealth avail him when he goes down?" The same verb, the same verdict.

Put together, the logic is airtight. The thing they are asking for — time, comfort, more of the world — is precisely the thing that will be worth nothing at the point where they will need something to be worth something.

## From the Sunnah: dipped once

Ibn Kathir supports this with a hadith he describes as authentic. (He does not name a collection here, so neither will I.) Its meaning is this: a disbeliever is brought and dipped into the Fire a single time, then asked whether he ever saw any good, whether he ever knew any comfort at all — and he answers, "No, by Allah, my Lord." Then the person who lived in the harshest misery on earth is brought and immersed for a brief spell in Paradise, then asked whether he ever knew any hardship — and he answers, "No, by Allah, my Lord."

Ibn Kathir's own summary of it is one phrase: **as if nothing ever happened.**

This is what ayah 207 means, made into an image. One dip erases a lifetime of pleasure so completely that the man cannot honestly recall a single good day. One moment erases a lifetime of misery just as completely. The Hereafter is not merely longer than this life; it re-prices everything the moment it arrives.

## Ayat 208–209: Allah has never been unjust

وَمَآ أَهْلَكْنَا مِن قَرْيَةٍ إِلَّا لَهَا مُنذِرُونَ ۝ ذِكْرَىٰ وَمَا كُنَّا ظَٰلِمِينَ

"We have never destroyed a society without warners, to remind them, for We would never wrong anyone."

Ibn Kathir reads these two ayat as Allah telling us of **His justice towards His creation**: He does not destroy any nation until after He has left them with no excuse — by warning them, by sending Messengers to them, and by establishing proof against them. He cites two parallels: *"We never punish until We have sent a Messenger"* (17:15), and that your Lord never destroys the towns until He sends to their mother town a Messenger reciting Our signs to them, and then only when the people thereof are wrongdoers (28:59).

So the warning is described as coming **by way of reminder** — dhikrā — and the ayah ends: **wa mā kunnā ẓālimīn**, "and We have never been unjust." Allah negates injustice of Himself absolutely. The destruction of a heedless nation, when it comes, comes only after the message has reached them and the proof has been established against them. The very passage that is most frightening is therefore also the one that most clearly closes the door on any complaint. No one arrives at that moment able to say, *I was never told.*

It is worth noticing that Ibn Kathir explains ayah 205 in the language of *respite* — "even if We delay the matter and give them respite" — the same thing the deniers will one day beg for. The years of ayah 205 are that respite, being spent right now.

## Living it: the other side of long life

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something easy to miss in a passage this severe. There is a hint here, it says, that **a long life in this world is a grace from Allah upon a person**. What ruins it is ingratitude: those who show no thankfulness for this grace and do not submit will find that this respite and grace will not be of any avail to them.

So the passage cuts two ways depending on who is reading it. To the one who denies, it says: your years are running out and they are buying you nothing. To the believer, it says: these same years are a grace being handed to you daily, and they can be spent on something that will still be worth something after the dip.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then records a striking practice. Imam Zuhrī related that Sayyidnā ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz used to recite this very verse every morning, holding his beard and addressing not the disbelievers, but **his own self**, with lines of poetry whose sense is: *O duped one* — your whole day is spent in negligence and your night in sleep, while death is inevitable for you; you are not awake among the alert and woken, nor are you the one who will get salvation from among the sleepers; you keep striving for things whose results will soon be unpleasant to you. That, the last line says, is how cattle live in this world.

That is the model of how to read ayat 205–209. A man of standing and security took the ayah about *their* years and applied it every morning to *his own*. The passage is aimed at the deniers; the sound response is to take the aim seriously and check whether the description fits before assuming it does not.

**In short:** ayah 205 offers the most generous possible terms — years of enjoyment. Ayah 206 lets the promised reckoning arrive. Ayah 207 totals up the account and finds it empty. And ayat 208–209 confirm that warners came by way of reminder, that no excuse was left standing, and that Allah has never been unjust.

passages.title: The devils did not bring this Qur'ān down
passages.tafsir:
