**The passage in one breath:** these three ayat shut the door on the idea that the Qur'an came from the devils. Ayah 210 denies it outright; ayah 211 gives two reasons rooted in the devils themselves — they would not want to and they could not; ayah 212 gives a third reason rooted in Allah's own action — they are held away from even hearing it. Read together they are a single, tightly built argument, and what holds them together is that each clause closes off one more escape route until nothing is left of the accusation.

## Where these ayat stand

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on this passage by describing what kind of Book this is: a Book "which falsehood cannot approach from before or behind it, sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise." And he states its true channel of descent: it was brought down by "the trustworthy Rūḥ" — that is, Jibrīl — "who is helped by Allah."

That framing matters. The denial in ayah 210 is not a bare negation floating in the air. It is one half of a pair: not the devils — but Jibrīl, the trustworthy one, supported by Allah. Ibn Kathir's heading for this whole passage says exactly that: *The Qur'an Was Brought Down by Jibrīl, Not Shayṭān*.

## Ayah 210 — "It was not the devils who brought this down"

**وَمَا تَنَزَّلَتۡ بِهِ ٱلشَّيَٰطِينُ**

The question this ayah answers is not only "where did this text come from?" but "who carried it down?" — and the answer given here is first a denial: not the Shayāṭīn, the devils.

Notice, too, that this is not a denial about a single moment. Ibn Kathir speaks of "the time when the Qur'an was being revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ" — a stretch of time, a long process of descent, portion after portion. The denial covers all of it. As Ibn Kathir will put it a few lines later, not "even one letter of it" came that way.

And having denied, Ibn Kathir immediately supplies the positive answer he opened with: the carrier was the trustworthy Rūḥ, Jibrīl, helped by Allah. The accusation is not simply refused; it is replaced with the truth.

## Ayah 211 — the two reasons inside the devils themselves

**وَمَا يَنۢبَغِي لَهُمۡ وَمَا يَسۡتَطِيعُونَ** — "it is not for them to do so, nor can they."

Ibn Kathir says Allah gives **three reasons** why it could not have been the devils who brought the Qur'an down. Two of them are here, and they are of completely different kinds — one about will, one about power.

**Reason one: it would not suit them.** *Mā yanbaghī lahum* — "neither would it suit them." Ibn Kathir explains: "they have no desire to do so and they do not want to, because their nature is to corrupt and misguide people, but this contains words enjoining what is right and forbidding what is evil, and light, guidance and mighty proofs. There is a big difference between this and the Shayāṭīn."

This is an argument from character, and it is devastating precisely because it is so ordinary. Ask what the Qur'an actually *does*. It commands good. It forbids evil. It is light, guidance, and mighty proof. Now ask what devils actually *want*: corruption and misguidance. A thing is known by what it produces. Nobody works relentlessly to destroy what he has spent his whole effort building. A Book whose entire content pulls in the opposite direction from a devil's entire purpose cannot be that devil's own delivery. The gap is not narrow — Ibn Kathir calls it "a big difference."

**Reason two: nor are they able.** *Wa mā yastaṭīʿūn.* Ibn Kathir's gloss is blunt: "even if they wanted to, they could not do it." Grant them the desire for the sake of argument — grant every one of them a sudden hunger to carry down words of light — and the answer is still no. The capacity is not there.

To make that felt, Ibn Kathir cites Allah's word:

> "Had We sent down this Qur'an on a mountain, you would surely have seen it humbling itself and rent asunder by the fear of Allah" (59:21).

Sit with the image. A mountain — the very picture of immovable solidity — would buckle and split under the weight of this speech. If the mass of a mountain could not bear it, what is a devil going to do with it? The verse does not merely say the devils are weak; it recalibrates our sense of what the Qur'an *is*. We handle it in printed pages and recite it in a few minutes and forget its weight. Ayah 211 quietly restores that weight.

Notice also how the two denials are ordered: will first, then power. Even the wanting is impossible; and even if the wanting were granted, the doing is impossible. Two short, absolute refusals, one after the other — no argumentation, no build-up.

## Ayah 212 — the third reason, and it is Allah's own doing

**إِنَّهُمۡ عَنِ ٱلسَّمۡعِ لَمَعۡزُولُونَ** — "for they are strictly barred from even overhearing it"; in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "Verily, they have been removed far from hearing it."

The first two reasons were about what the devils are. This one is about what was done to them.

Ibn Kathir explains: "even if they wanted to and were able to bear it and convey it, they still would not be able to achieve that, because they were prevented from hearing the Qur'an when it was brought down, for the heavens were filled with guardians and shooting stars at the time when the Qur'an was being revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so none of the Shayāṭīn could hear even one letter of it, **lest there be any confusion in the matter**."

That last phrase is the heart of it. Suppose a devil had caught even a single letter as it descended, and passed it to someone on earth who put it about before the Qur'an itself reached the people. Doubt would have been planted at the root: *we heard that from another source first.* The matter would have been muddied. So the route was sealed at the source.

And note where the sealing comes from. The ayah does not say the devils simply kept their distance; it says they *have been removed*. Ibn Kathir names the guarded heavens as "a part of Allah's mercy towards His servants, protection of His Laws, and support for His Book and His Messenger ﷺ" — so this barring is Allah's own doing, an act on His side of the ledger, not a failure on theirs. The devils are not merely bad at eavesdropping. They have been put out of the channel altogether. And what they are barred from is the *hearing* itself — not one letter reached them.

Ibn Kathir supports this with what Allah reports about the jinn — their own testimony, in their own words:

> "And we have sought to reach the heaven; but found it filled with stern guards and flaming fires. And verily, we used to sit there in stations, to (steal) a hearing, but any who listens now will find a flaming fire watching him in ambush." (72:8-10)

Two details stand out. They admit there *used* to be listening posts — "stations" they would sit in — so this was a real route once. And they admit the route is now closed: "any who listens **now**" is met by fire lying in wait. The change is dated, and Ibn Kathir dates it to the time this revelation was descending. He carries the citation onward to the jinn's closing words — "or whether their Lord intends for them a right path" — so their own account ends by reaching for what their Lord intends. They could see the guard posted; the purpose behind it was His.

## Why this is described as mercy

Ibn Kathir does not leave the guarded heaven as a piece of cosmology. He names what it is for: "This is a part of Allah's mercy towards His servants, protection of His Laws, and support for His Book and His Messenger ﷺ."

Three benefits, each worth naming:

- **Mercy towards His servants** — because a person seeking guidance is spared the torment of never knowing whether what reached him is revelation or interference.
- **Protection of His Laws** — the sacred law rests on this text; corrupt the text at the point of delivery and everything built on it is corrupted with it.
- **Support for His Book and His Messenger ﷺ** — with the channel sealed, no rival "source" could ever be produced to compete with what he brought.

So the guarded sky is not decoration. It is part of how Allah preserved this revelation, running silently above while the revelation came down.

## The shape of the argument

Three doors, closed one after another, in a rising order of finality:

1. **They would not** — it does not suit their nature (ayah 211, first half).
2. **They could not** — even granting the will, the power is absent (ayah 211, second half).
3. **They were not even allowed near** — the channel itself was sealed (ayah 212).

Any one of the three would settle the matter. Allah gives three, which is itself instructive: this is a claim He chose to bury, not merely to answer. And notice the movement — from the devils' character, to the devils' capacity, to Allah's own decisive act. The argument ends not with what creation is like but with what Allah did. That is where certainty properly rests.

## Living it

**Take the Qur'an's weight seriously.** Ayah 211 makes its point with a mountain that would humble itself and split apart. The next time you open the muṣḥaf casually, let that image return. What you are holding would have rent a mountain in the telling.

**Judge a message by what it produces.** Ibn Kathir's first argument is one an ordinary believer can use daily: look at what a message actually calls you to. Does it enjoin what is right and forbid what is evil, does it carry light and guidance and mighty proof — or does it corrupt and mislead? Speech shows its origin in its direction of travel. A voice that consistently pulls you toward corruption is telling you where it came from, whatever it claims about itself.

**Rest in the preservation.** You do not have to wonder whether some fragment of what you recite slipped in from a stolen listening post. The heavens were filled with guardians and shooting stars for exactly that reason — so that not one letter could be overheard, "lest there be any confusion in the matter" — and Ibn Kathir names it as mercy toward you. Recite with the confidence of someone holding what arrived clean: brought down by the trustworthy Rūḥ, and guarded the whole way down.

passages.title: Warn your kin and trust in the Almighty
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are one continuous charge from Allah to His Messenger ﷺ, and they read best as a single instruction rather than as separate verses: worship Me alone — warn the people closest to you — be kind to those who follow you — declare yourself clear of the deeds of those who refuse — and then put your whole weight on Me, because I see you and I hear you. What holds the unit together is that movement from the mission outward (ayat 213–216) to the One who stands behind the missionary (ayat 217–220).

Ibn Kathir reads the run exactly this way. He says that here Allah commands the Prophet ﷺ to worship Him alone with no partner or associate and tells him that whoever associates others with Him in worship will be punished; then commands him to warn his tribe of near kindred — those most closely related to him — and to tell them that nothing could save any one of them except faith in Allah; then commands him to be kind and gentle with the believing servants of Allah who followed him, and to disown those who disobeyed him, no matter who they were.

## Ayah 213: the ground everything else stands on

"So, invoke not with Allah another god lest you should be among those who receive punishment." Before any command to call others, there is a command about oneself. The one carrying the warning must first be free of the very thing he warns against. And notice how the consequence is phrased: not "you will be punished" but "lest you should be among those who receive punishment" — the Messenger ﷺ himself, hypothetically, placed in the same ranks as everyone else, under the same rule. There is no protected class in this religion. That is precisely the point he ﷺ will make to Fāṭimah his daughter and to Ṣafiyyah daughter of 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib a few lines later.

## Ayah 214: the call from aṣ-Ṣafā

This is the ayah the sources open up most. Ibn Kathir says many hadiths have been narrated concerning the revelation of this ayah, and he quotes several.

**The first.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said that when Allah revealed *"And warn your tribe of near kindred,"* the Prophet ﷺ went to aṣ-Ṣafā, climbed up and called out *"Yā ṣabāḥāh!"* — rendered in the source as *"O people!"*, the same call he raises again in the third narration below, where he likens himself to a man who has spotted an enemy. The people gathered around him, some coming of their own accord and others sending people on their behalf to find out what was happening. He ﷺ said: "O Banī 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib, O Banī Fihr, O Banī Lu'ayy! What do you think, if I told you that there was a cavalry at the foot of this mountain coming to attack you — would you believe me?" They said, "Yes." He said: "Then I warn you of a great punishment that is close at hand."

Look at what he ﷺ has done. He has not started with an argument. He has started by asking them to audit their own experience of him: *you know I do not lie to you about a raid; so weigh what I am about to say by that same standard.* Their own "yes" is the evidence he uses.

Then Abū Lahab said, "May you perish for the rest of the day! You only called us to tell us this?" And Allah revealed *"Perish the two hands of Abū Lahab and perish he!"* (111:1). Ibn Kathir notes this narration was also recorded by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasā'ī.

So the very first response to the very first public warning was contempt. Ayah 216 — *"if they disobey you"* — is not a distant hypothetical. It was the weather of that very gathering.

**The second.** Imam Ahmad recorded that 'Ā'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said that when this ayah was revealed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up and said: "O Fāṭimah daughter of Muhammad, O Ṣafiyyah daughter of 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib, O Banī 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib, I cannot help you before Allah. Ask me for whatever you want of my wealth." Ibn Kathir says this was recorded by Muslim.

This is the sharpest thing in the passage. He names his own daughter first. He offers them everything he owns, and tells them plainly that the one thing he cannot give them is help before Allah. Nearness to the Prophet ﷺ by blood buys nothing there; only faith does. That is Ibn Kathir's summary of the command itself — he was to tell them that nothing could save any of them except faith in Allah.

**The third.** Imam Ahmad recorded from Qabīṣah bin Mukhāriq and Zuhayr bin 'Amr that when the ayah was revealed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ climbed on top of a rock on the side of a mountain and started to call out: "O Banī 'Abd Manāf, I am indeed a warner, and the parable of me and you is that of a man who sees the enemy so he goes to save his family, fearing that the enemy may reach them before he does." And he started to call out, "Yā ṣabāḥāh!" — "O people!" Ibn Kathir says this was also recorded by Muslim and an-Nasā'ī.

That parable explains the tone of every warning in the Qur'an. A man who has seen the enemy and is running does not sound calm — and he does not run to strangers first, he runs home. The urgency in his voice is not hostility; it is love in a hurry. And the fear inside the parable is the fear of arriving *late*: "fearing that the enemy may reach them before he does."

## Why start with your own family?

*Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān* takes up the obvious question. *'Ashīrah* (عشيرة) means clan, and limiting it with *al-aqrabīn* — "the nearest people" — makes it refer to close relatives. But the Prophet's ﷺ mission as a messenger is universal to the whole Ummah. So what is the wisdom in making it special for the members of the clan?

The answer given is that, looked at closely, this is an easy and effective way of preaching with far-reaching effect, and the reasons are drawn out of ordinary human experience:

- **Priority.** One's own family members, having the privilege of closeness, are entitled to precedence over others when any act of virtue is being initiated.
- **Credibility.** By virtue of close mutual relations, relatives know each other well, and anyone with false claims would get exposed in no time. Conversely, the one with a good reputation among his family members would be readily accepted and listened to. (This is exactly what the crowd's "yes" at aṣ-Ṣafā demonstrated.)
- **Momentum.** Once close relatives throw their weight behind a good cause, it brings unity and mutual help between them; that group, built on trust and sincerity, then works "like a small power" in spreading the precepts of religion to others.
- **Environment.** The point is put bluntly. Following good conduct and morals and sticking to them is only possible when the environment is favourable. If only one person in an entire household wishes to perform his prayers regularly, even that devotee will find it difficult to carry it out. And it has become difficult to abstain from unlawful things not because keeping away from them is impossible, but because when the whole fraternity is involved in a sin, it becomes very difficult for just one person to keep himself aloof.

This is tied to *"Save yourself and your family members from the fire of Jahannam"* (66:6): the responsibility of saving one's dependants from that Fire is placed on every member of the clan, and this is an easy and simple way of reforming conduct and morals — start with the people in your own house.

And there is a long view. When this verse was revealed the Prophet ﷺ called out all the members of his family and conveyed to them the message of truth. They did not accept the truth at that time — but gradually the family members started coming into Islam, and when his uncle Sayyidunā Ḥamzah (may Allah be pleased with him) accepted Islam it provided great strength to the mission. The call that looked like a failure on the day it was made was not a failure. It was a seed.

**On the scope of the warning.** Ibn Kathir anticipates a worry: does a *specific* command to warn near relatives limit the *general* mission? He says no — this specific warning does not contradict the general warning; indeed it is a part of it. He lines up ayah after ayah showing the reach of the Prophet's ﷺ warning: *"in order that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless"* (36:6); *"that you may warn the Mother of the Towns and all around it"* (42:7); *"and warn therewith those who fear that they will be gathered before their Lord"* (6:51); *"that you may give glad tidings to those who have taqwā, and warn with it the most quarrelsome people"* (19:97); *"that I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach"* (6:19); and *"but those of the sects that reject it, the Fire will be their promised meeting place"* (11:17). He then cites Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet ﷺ said: "By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, no one from these nations — Jewish or Christian — hears of me then does not believe in me, but he will enter Hell." The circle starts at Banī 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib; it does not end there.

## Ayah 215: be kind to those who follow you

*"And be kind and humble to the believers who follow you"* — or, as the passage translation renders it, *"and be gracious to the believers who follow you."* Ibn Kathir gives the sense as being kind and gentle with the believing servants of Allah who followed him.

Its placement is the lesson. It sits directly between the hard public warning of ayah 214 and the disavowal of ayah 216. The same voice that raises the alarm from the mountain must go soft the instant someone answers it. Severity belongs to the danger, never to the people who have come to you. Whoever takes one step toward the truth should find kindness, not scrutiny.

## Ayah 216: clear of what you do

*"Then if they disobey you, say: I am innocent of what you do."* Ibn Kathir's gloss is that he was commanded to disown those who disobeyed him, no matter who they were — and "no matter who they were" is doing serious work, given the narrations we have just read about who answered that call and how.

Notice the exact wording the Qur'an puts in his mouth: innocent of *what you do*. The disavowal is fastened to the deeds. He is not told to hate anyone, or to stop calling anyone; he is told to make it unmistakable that he does not stand behind their actions. This is where the passage releases him. He has warned. The outcome was never his to control.

## Ayah 217: put your trust in the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful

Then comes the pivot. Having been told to warn people who may well refuse him, and to disown their deeds, he is told where to put his weight: *wa tawakkal 'alā-l-'Azīz ar-Raḥīm.* Ibn Kathir explains it as trust in all your affairs, "for He is your Helper, Protector and Supporter, and He is the One Who will cause you to prevail and will make your word supreme."

The two names are worth pausing over. *Al-'Azīz*, the All-Mighty — the One who, as Ibn Kathir says, will cause His Messenger ﷺ to prevail and make his word supreme. *Ar-Raḥīm*, the Most Merciful — the One who is his Helper, Protector and Supporter. Power without care would be terrifying; care without power would be sentimental. Trust is only rational when both are true of the One trusted — and Allah names Himself by both in a single breath, at exactly the moment His Messenger ﷺ is most exposed.

## Ayat 218–219: the eye that never leaves you

*"Who sees you when you stand up, and your movements among those who fall prostrate."* Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 218 is warm: it means He is taking care of you. He compares it to *"So wait patiently for the decision of your Lord, for verily, you are under Our Eyes"* (52:48). Being seen by Allah, here, is not surveillance — it is care.

The early authorities differed over what precise "standing" is meant, and Ibn Kathir simply lists their readings rather than settling on one:

- **Ibn 'Abbās**: it means "to pray."
- **'Ikrimah**: "He sees him when he stands and bows and prostrates."
- **Al-Ḥasan**: "when you pray alone."
- **Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk**: "when you are lying in bed and when you are sitting."
- **Qatādah**: "when you are standing, when you are sitting, and in all other situations."

The readings run along a spectrum, from the most focused (the standing of ṣalāh) to the most expansive (every posture of your day, right down to lying in bed at night). The difference among them is over what this ayah is pointing at.

For ayah 219 — *"and your movements among those who fall prostrate"* — Qatādah read the two ayat together as covering prayer in both of its forms: "when you pray, He sees you when you pray alone and when you pray in congregation." Ibn Kathir notes this was also the view of 'Ikrimah, 'Aṭā' al-Khurāsānī and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.

There is real comfort in that pairing for a man told to warn people who might turn on him. The Qur'an does not answer his exposure by promising him a crowd. It answers: *I see you when you stand alone, and I see you when you move among them.* Whether the room is full or empty, the attention that matters is unchanged.

## Ayah 220: He, only He, is the All-Hearer, the All-Knower

The passage seals that thought with two names. Ibn Kathir: He hears all that His servants say and He knows all their movements — and he cites *"Neither you do any deed nor recite any portion of the Qur'an, nor you do any deed, but We are Witness thereof, when you are doing it"* (10:61).

Hearing answers the words — including words like the ones thrown at him the day he stood up to warn. Knowing answers the deeds. Between the two, nothing that happened on that mountain, and nothing that happens in your life, falls outside Allah's notice. The Prophet ﷺ is being told: you are not calling out into an empty sky.

## Living it

- **Start at home.** *Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān* makes this the practical heart of the passage: your family has precedence when you initiate any act of virtue, and the strongest protection for your own religion is a household where practising it is normal rather than lonely.
- **Earn the "yes" first.** The Prophet ﷺ built his warning on a reputation his relatives had already tested. Credibility with the people who see you every day is not a side matter; it is the platform.
- **Speak like someone who has seen the enemy.** Urgency out of love rather than anger — and out of the fear of arriving too late.
- **Then be gentle.** The moment someone responds, be kind and humble with them. Alarm for the danger; softness for the people.
- **Say your piece and let go.** Your responsibility is the warning and the manner of it. *"I am innocent of what you do"* is permission to stop carrying an outcome that was never yours.
- **Be patient with slow results.** They did not accept the truth on the day. Ḥamzah came later, and the family came in gradually.
- **Do it all under His eye.** Standing, sitting, alone or in the row — the same Seeing, Hearing, Knowing Lord, *al-'Azīz ar-Raḥīm*, is the One you are actually working for, and the only One you need on your side.

passages.title: Not a soothsayer, and not a poet
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat close Sūrah ash-Shuʿarāʾ by answering, head-on, the two accusations the pagans of Makkah threw at the Prophet ﷺ: that his message reached him from the jinn, the way a soothsayer gets his information, or that he composed it himself, the way a poet composes. Ayat 221–223 dispose of the first charge, 224–226 of the second, and ayah 227 then rescues the believing poet from the censure and closes the surah with a warning aimed at every wrongdoer.

## The accusation being answered

Ibn Kathir sets the scene: Allah here addresses those idolators who claimed that what the Messenger ﷺ brought was not the truth, but was either something he had made up himself or something that came to him in visions from the jinn. Allah declares His Messenger far above their claims and fabrications: what he brought did indeed come from Allah, revelation and inspiration, **"brought down by a noble, trustworthy and mighty angel."** It did not come from the devils — "because they have no desire for anything like this Noble Qur'an. They descend upon those who are like them, the lying fortune-tellers."

## Ayat 221–223: the counter-question

**"Shall I inform you...?"** (221) — Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: *shall I tell you.*

Two words then describe the human host that devils seek out, and between them they cover a whole person:

- **affāk** — Ibn Kathir: "one whose speech is lies and fabrication." This is the tongue.
- **athīm** — Ibn Kathir: "whose deeds are immoral." This is the life behind the tongue.

"This is the person upon whom the Shayāṭīn descend: fortune-tellers and other sinful liars." And then the sentence that seals the logic: **"The Shayāṭīn are also sinful liars."** Like goes to like.

**"Who gives ear"** (223) — Ibn Kathir explains *yulqūn as-samʿ* as the eavesdropping itself: "they try to overhear what is said in the heavens, and they try to hear something of the Unseen, then they add to it a hundred lies and tell it to their human comrades, who then tell it to others. Then the people believe everything they say because they were right about the one thing which was heard from the heavens."

## From the Sunnah: how one true word buys a hundred lies

Ibn Kathir cites three narrations here, all attributed to Al-Bukhari.

**First**, from ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: people asked the Prophet ﷺ about fortune-tellers and he said, **"They are nothing."** They said, "O Messenger of Allah, they say things that come true." He said: **"That is a word of truth which the Jinn snatches, then he gabbles it like the clucking of a chicken into the ear of his friend, but he mixes it with more than one hundred lies."**

**Second**, from Abu Hurayrah, a longer picture of the chain of transmission: **"When Allah decrees a matter in heaven, the angels beat their wings in submission to His decree, a chain beating on a rock. And when the fear in their hearts subsides, they say: 'What is it that your Lord has said?' They say: 'The truth. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.'"** The listening jinn are stacked one above the other — the narrator Sufyan illustrated it by holding his hand vertically with his fingers outspread — and they throw the snatched word down from one to another until it is passed to the fortune-teller or soothsayer. A shooting star may strike the jinn before he passes it on, or he may pass it on before he is struck; and "he adds to it one hundred lies." Then it is said: "Did he not tell us that on such and such a day, such and such would happen?" — **"So they believe him because of that one thing which was heard from the heavens."**

**Third**, again from ʿĀ'ishah: **"The angels speak in the clouds about some matter on earth, and the Shayāṭīn overhear what they say, so they tell it to the fortune-teller, gurgling into his ear like (a liquid poured) from a glass bottle, and he adds to it one hundred lies."**

The Prophet's ﷺ verdict — "They are nothing" — was not a claim that fortune-tellers never say anything that comes true; he was told directly that they do, and still granted them no standing. The one snatched word is precisely what makes the hundred lies believable.

## Ayat 224–226: what a poet is, and why the Qur'an is not that

**What does *shiʿr* actually mean?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up carefully. *Shiʿr* — the root of *shuʿarāʾ*, "poets," and usually translated "poetry" — is an Arabic word that lexically means **any statement based on imagination and on ideas not confirmed by serious proofs**. To be *shiʿr* in that original Arabic sense, Maʿārif notes, it is not necessary to have a particular rhythm, or *qāfiyah*, or *radīf*. Because such imaginative speech was in practice always composed on particular rhythms, the technical definition settled as "a composition of words having a particular rhythm and a similar sound at the end of each line (*Qāfiyah*)."

That double meaning matters, because the pagans of Makkah called the Prophet ﷺ a *shāʿir* and the Qur'an *shiʿr*, and the commentators differ over which sense they intended. Maʿārif reports both views:

- **Some commentators** hold they meant it technically — that they were calling the Qur'an poetry in the technical sense.
- **Others** hold it was not so, because the infidels of Makkah were fully conversant with the code and principles of poetry, and the Qur'an is obviously not a book of poetry. "Even a non-Arab would not accept that, not to say anything of the eloquent Arabs." On this view they called him a poet in the *literal* sense of the word — that is, they regarded his thoughts as imaginary. Their objective was to call him a liar, since the word *shāʿir* is also used in the sense of a lie, and *shiʿr* for a liar.

**Within ayah 224 itself,** Maʿārif takes *shāʿir* in its technical and commonly known meaning — the rhythmic composer — and cites as support the narration in Fatḥ al-Bārī about the Companions who were poets (below). On that reading, the poets censured at the opening of the verse are the *disbelieving* poets, "because depraved people, defiant Shaitan and disobedient Jinn followed and narrated their poetry."

**"The astray ones follow them"** (224). ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that this means "the disbelievers follow the misguided among mankind and the Jinn" — the view also of Mujāhid, ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam and others. ʿIkrimah gives the social picture behind it: two poets would ridicule one another in verse, one group of people supporting one and another group supporting the other, and Allah revealed the ayah about that. Al-ʿAwfī reported the same scene from Ibn ʿAbbās — in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, two men, one from the Anṣār and one from another tribe, ridiculing one another in verse, each backed by a group of his own people, "who were the foolish ones."

**"See you not that they speak about every subject in their poetry?"** (225) — so Ibn Kathir's text renders it; the translation supplied with the passage reads, "Do you not see how they rant in every field." Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah: "They indulge in every kind of nonsense." Through aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk: "They engage in every kind of verbal art." This was also the view of Mujāhid and others. Either way the charge is the same: a tongue that ranges over anything at all.

**"And they say what they do not do"** (226). The poet's word floats free of his life. Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion plainly: the Messenger ﷺ to whom this Qur'an was revealed was not a soothsayer or a poet, "because his situation was quite obviously different to theirs." He cites Allah's own words: **"And We have not taught him poetry, nor is it suitable for him. This is only a Reminder and a plain Qur'an"** (36:69), and **"It is not the word of a poet, little is that you believe! Nor is it the word of a soothsayer, little is that you remember! This is the Revelation sent down from the Lord of all that exists"** (69:40–43).

## Ayah 227: the exception, and the weeping poets

**"Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and remember Allah much, and vindicate themselves after they have been wronged."**

Ibn Kathir relates it through this chain: Muḥammad bin Isḥāq narrated from Yazīd bin ʿAbdullāh bin Qusayṭ, that Abū al-Ḥasan Sālim al-Barrād, the freed servant of Tamīm ad-Dārī, said that when the verse about the poets was revealed, **Ḥassān bin Thābit, ʿAbdullāh bin Rawāḥah and Kaʿb bin Mālik** came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ **weeping**, and said: "Allah knew when He revealed this Ayah that we are poets." The Prophet ﷺ recited to them the exception, clause by clause:

- "Except those who believe and do righteous deeds" — **"you."**
- "and remember Allah much" — **"you."**
- "and vindicate themselves after they have been wronged" — **"you."**

Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr from Ibn Isḥāq's narration. Maʿārif cites the version in Fatḥ al-Bārī, where the Prophet ﷺ told them, "You go through the last part of the verse" — conveying that their poetry was not frivolous or ill-intentioned, so they were included in the exception mentioned at the end of the verse.

**Ibn Kathir's honest caveat.** He does not let the moving story pass unexamined: "But this Surah was revealed in Makkah, so how could the reason for its revelation be the poets of the Anṣār? This is something worth thinking about. The reports that have been narrated about this are all *Mursal* and cannot be relied on. And Allah knows best." (*Mursal* is a technical term for a report whose chain has a missing link at the Companion level, so it does not reach back through an eyewitness.) There is a lesson in the method itself: a scholar can transmit a beloved report and still tell you frankly what its chain is worth.

The *scope* of the exception stands regardless. Ibn Kathir continues that it could include the poets of the Anṣār **and others** — it even includes those poets of the Jāhiliyyah who had indulged in condemning Islam and its followers, then repented and turned to Allah, gave up what they used to do, started to do righteous deeds and remember Allah much, and praised Islam and its followers in order to make up for their insults, "for good deeds wipe out bad deeds." He gives two faces to this:

- **ʿAbdullāh bin az-Zabʿarī**, who said on becoming Muslim: "O Messenger of Allah, indeed my tongue will try to make up for things it said when I was bad — When I went along with the Shayṭān during the years of misguidance, and whoever inclines towards his way is in a state of loss."
- **Abū Sufyān bin al-Ḥārith bin ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib**, the Prophet's own cousin, who had been among the most hostile of people to him and mocked him more than anyone. But when he became Muslim, "there was no one more beloved to him than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He began to praise the Messenger of Allah ﷺ where he had mocked him, and take him as a close friend where he had regarded him as an enemy."

The same tongue, re-aimed.

**"And vindicate themselves after they have been wronged."** Ibn ʿAbbās explained: "They responded in kind to the disbelievers who used to ridicule the believers in verse" — the view also of Mujāhid, Qatādah and several others. It was also recorded in the Sahih that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Ḥassān, **"Ridicule them in verse,"** or, in the other wording, **"Ridicule them in verse, and Jibrīl is with you."** And Imam Aḥmad recorded that when Kaʿb bin Mālik said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Allah has revealed what He revealed about the poets," he replied: **"The believer wages Jihad with his sword and with his tongue. By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, it is as if you are attacking them with arrows."**

## The place of poetry in the Sharīʿah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the balance out at length. At the beginning of these verses poetry is disapproved strongly; the exception allowed towards the end of the surah proves that poetry is not condemned completely.

**What is condemned** is poetry that encourages disobedience to Allah, puts a hindrance in His remembrance, falsely disgraces or condemns someone, or is obscene or leads to obscenity. Poetry free of these things is exonerated by the exception in ayah 227.

**What is praised** is poetry dealing with the subjects of wisdom based on sermons and teachings — part of the virtues carrying reward in the Hereafter. Maʿārif cites the report of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, *"There is a poetry which contains wisdom"* (Bukhari). Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar said that "wisdom" here stands for rightful things based on truth; Ibn Baṭṭāl explained that poetry dealing with the Oneness of Allah, His remembrance and love for Islam is desirable and praiseworthy and is the type in view in that hadith, while poetry dealing with falsehood and obscenity is contemptible.

Maʿārif then lines up the practice of the early community: ʿAmr ibn Sharīd reported through his father that the Prophet ﷺ listened to a hundred couplets of Umayyah ibn as-Salt from him; Muṭarrif reported travelling with ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn from Kufa to Basrah while he recited couplets at every stage of the journey; Ṭabarī reported that the distinguished Companions and Tābiʿīn used to compose, listen to and recite poetry; Imam Bukhari reported that Sayyidah ʿĀ'ishah used to compose poetry; and Abū Yaʿlā reported from Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ said, **"Poetry is a composition"** — if its subject matter is good and useful it is good, and if its subject is bad or sinful it is bad. Al-Qurṭubī adds that among the ten famous jurists of Madinah, ʿUbaydullāh ibn ʿUtbah ibn Masʿūd was an eloquently articulate poet, and quotes Abū ʿAmr that no intelligent and knowledgeable person would take poetry of nice subjects as bad. Maʿārif also notes that among the noble Companions who were the religious leaders, there is none who had either not composed poetry himself or not recited or listened to the composition of others with fondness.

**So why the severe narrations?** Maʿārif answers: where poetry is condemned in certain narrations, the purpose is that one should not get so engrossed in it that he neglects his worship and the Qur'an. Imam Bukhari treated this in a separate chapter, quoting Abu Hurayrah: *"It is better to fill up one's belly with pus than to fill it up with poetry."* Bukhari's own understanding, Maʿārif reports, is that this statement portrays the situation where poetry becomes dominant over the remembrance of Allah, over one's involvement with the Qur'an, or over acquiring knowledge — but if poetry is kept under check, it is not bad. Alongside that, there is consensus of the Ummah that obscene or defaming poetry is unlawful and not permitted, and Qurṭubī notes this ruling is not exclusive to poetry: it applies to any writing, prose or verse.

The early authorities enforced it. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb dismissed his governor ʿAdiyy ibn Naḍlah from his position because he used to compose obscene poetry. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz directed that ʿAmr ibn Rabīʿah and Abū al-Aḥwaṣ be exiled on the same charge — and when ʿAmr ibn Rabīʿah repented of his deeds, his repentance was accepted.

**The principle that outlives poetry.** Ibn Abī Jamrah ruled that excessive involvement in poetry, and all such learning or art as makes one oblivious of the remembrance of Allah, causes doubts in the mind about the beliefs of Islam, or helps promote spiritual ills, falls under the same ruling as is given for contemptible poetry.

## Are leaders answerable for their followers?

Maʿārif raises a fair question about ayah 224: the poets are blamed here for their followers being misled, so how can they be blamed for what their followers adopt? The answer is that the wrong deeds adopted by followers are normally a sign of the misdeeds of the one who is followed. But Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī clarified that this rule applies where the one followed has a hand in it — if there is no check on lying and backbiting in his gatherings, and those who sit in his company pick up the habit, their sin is regarded as a manifestation of his. Where the followers' misdeeds are different from the leader's own deeds, he cannot be made responsible: a person may follow a scholar diligently and sincerely in belief and still not follow him in righteous deeds and morals, and the scholar cannot be blamed for that. (Allah is pure and knows best.)

## The closing warning

**"And those who do wrong will come to know by what overturning they will be overturned"** (227). Ibn Kathir sets it beside **"The Day when their excuses will be of no profit to wrongdoers"** (40:52), and cites what is in the Sahih: **"Beware of wrongdoing, for wrongdoing will be darkness on the Day of Resurrection."** Qatādah bin Diʿāmah said this closing threat refers to the poets and others.

The devils descend on the liar whose deeds match his tongue; revelation came down by a noble, trustworthy and mighty angel. The poets say what they do not do; the exception is for those who believe, act, remember Allah much — and only then answer back.
